options.label: MED specifies the destination transport port
options.explanation: Incorrect — It is a routing attribute and does not demultiplex applications.

options.label: MED measures TLS handshake duration in milliseconds
options.explanation: Incorrect — Despite its name, the value is not an observed latency timer.

stem: How does CLUSTER_LIST help prevent loops among BGP route reflectors?

options.label: It lists every client IP currently using the route
options.explanation: Incorrect — CLUSTER_LIST records reflector clusters, not traffic endpoints.

options.label: A reflector rejects an update whose CLUSTER_LIST contains its own cluster ID
options.explanation: Correct — The accumulated cluster path exposes reflection loops analogously to path-loop detection.

options.label: It encrypts updates between reflectors
options.explanation: Incorrect — Loop metadata does not provide transport confidentiality.

options.label: It replaces AS_PATH for external routing
options.explanation: Incorrect — Route reflection augments internal BGP and retains AS_PATH semantics.

stem: What does RPKI-based BGP origin validation check for a received route?

options.label: Whether every AS in the path used the shortest physical cable
options.explanation: Incorrect — RPKI origin validation does not attest path geometry.

options.label: Whether the destination web server has a valid TLS certificate
options.explanation: Incorrect — Routing authorization and service endpoint certificates are separate trust systems.

options.label: Whether a Route Origin Authorization permits the origin AS to announce that prefix length
options.explanation: Correct — Origin validation compares the prefix and originating AS with cryptographically validated authorization data.

options.label: Whether packets on the route will never be dropped
options.explanation: Incorrect — Valid origin authorization makes no availability guarantee.

stem: Why can an aggregate route continue attracting traffic after the component route for a failed destination disappears?

options.label: TCP automatically recreates the missing subnet
options.explanation: Incorrect — Transport recovery cannot create network-layer reachability.

options.label: DNS converts the aggregate into a CNAME
options.explanation: Incorrect — Routing prefixes and DNS aliases are unrelated objects.

options.label: TLS selects a new prefix during certificate validation
options.explanation: Incorrect — PKI does not modify forwarding tables.

options.label: The less-specific aggregate still matches, so traffic follows it unless the aggregator has a valid internal path or discard route
options.explanation: Correct — Aggregation hides component reachability changes from upstream routers.

stem: A NAT uses endpoint-independent mapping for UDP. What remains stable when one internal socket sends to different external destinations?

options.label: The external mapped address and port for that internal address and port
options.explanation: Correct — Endpoint-independent mapping reuses one public mapping regardless of remote endpoint.

options.label: The destination server address is rewritten to the first server
options.explanation: Incorrect — The NAT preserves each intended remote destination.

options.label: Every response is accepted from any external host
options.explanation: Incorrect — Inbound filtering behavior is a separate property from mapping behavior.

options.label: The application payload becomes identical
options.explanation: Incorrect — Mapping affects endpoint translation, not message contents.

stem: How can Packetization Layer PMTUD recover when ICMP Packet Too Big messages are filtered?

options.label: Assume the largest possible packet always works
options.explanation: Incorrect — A fixed maximum can repeatedly black-hole traffic on a smaller path.

options.label: Probe candidate packet sizes and infer loss using acknowledgements or protocol-specific feedback
options.explanation: Correct — PLPMTUD does not depend solely on network-layer ICMP delivery.

options.label: Lower the DNS TTL until packets fit
options.explanation: Incorrect — Naming cache lifetimes do not affect packet size.

options.label: Disable retransmission so loss is invisible
options.explanation: Incorrect — Loss feedback is necessary to validate probe sizes and recover.

stem: Why is consistent hashing useful when backend membership changes for a cache-like service?

options.label: It guarantees perfectly equal request cost on every backend
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hash balance cannot account for arbitrary key popularity or work duration.

options.label: It detects application health without probes
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hash placement and health assessment are distinct mechanisms.

options.label: It remaps only a fraction of keys instead of reshuffling nearly every key
options.explanation: Correct — Limited disruption preserves cache locality as hosts join or leave.

options.label: It encrypts keys before they cross the network
options.explanation: Incorrect — Consistent hashing is a placement method, not cryptography.

stem: After withdrawing an unhealthy anycast site's route, why might some clients briefly continue sending traffic toward it?

options.label: TLS certificates force packets to the withdrawn site
options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificates authenticate endpoints and do not select routes.

options.label: DNS NXDOMAIN responses contain the old anycast path
options.explanation: Incorrect — Anycast path selection can occur without changing DNS answers.

options.label: TCP requires every route withdrawal to wait for TIME-WAIT
options.explanation: Incorrect — BGP convergence and endpoint TIME-WAIT are independent processes.

options.label: Routing updates converge asynchronously and cached forwarding state does not change everywhere at once
options.explanation: Correct — Anycast failover inherits the distributed convergence behavior of its routing system.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authenticator and Verifier Requirements

stem: A leaked password table contains two users with the same password. Which storage design prevents their verifier values from matching?

options.label: A unique random salt for each password
options.explanation: Correct — A per-password salt makes equal passwords produce different verifier values and defeats shared precomputation.

options.label: One application-wide initialization vector
options.explanation: Incorrect — A shared IV does not provide the per-record uniqueness required of password salts.

options.label: Base64-encoding each password
options.explanation: Incorrect — Encoding is reversible representation and adds no resistance to password guessing.

options.label: Truncating each verifier to 64 bits
options.explanation: Incorrect — Truncation increases collision and guessing risk rather than separating equal passwords.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authenticator and Verifier Requirements

stem: What is the main security purpose of a password-hashing cost factor?

options.label: Prevent the password from crossing TLS
options.explanation: Incorrect — The password still reaches the verifier over an authenticated protected channel.

options.label: Make every offline password guess more expensive
options.explanation: Correct — The adjustable work factor raises the attacker cost of testing each guessed password after a verifier leak.

options.label: Make all password hashes globally unique
options.explanation: Incorrect — Uniqueness comes from salts, not from the work factor.

options.label: Allow recovery of a forgotten password
options.explanation: Incorrect — Password verifiers should support checking, not plaintext recovery.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authenticator and Verifier Requirements

stem: A signup service wants to reject passwords commonly found in breaches. Which check matches current NIST guidance?

options.label: Require one symbol in every password
options.explanation: Incorrect — Composition rules do not specifically detect known-compromised passwords.

options.label: Force a password change every 30 days
options.explanation: Incorrect — Periodic changes are not the recommended response without evidence of compromise.

options.label: Compare the full proposed password with a blocklist
options.explanation: Correct — NIST calls for comparing the complete password against commonly used, expected, or compromised values.

options.label: Reject every dictionary substring
options.explanation: Incorrect — Substring rules reject many usable passwords and are not the specified blocklist check.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authenticator and Verifier Requirements

stem: Which authenticator property most directly provides phishing resistance?

options.label: A six-digit code that expires in 30 seconds
options.explanation: Incorrect — Short expiry limits time but a code can still be relayed by a phishing site.

options.label: A password longer than 20 characters
options.explanation: Incorrect — Password length does not bind the password to the intended verifier.

options.label: A security question known only to the user
options.explanation: Incorrect — Knowledge-based answers are reusable secrets and are not phishing-resistant.

options.label: Cryptographic binding to the legitimate verifier
options.explanation: Correct — Verifier-name or channel binding prevents an authenticator output captured by an impostor from working at the real verifier.

stem: Why can a WebAuthn credential registered for one relying party resist use on a lookalike domain?

options.label: The credential is scoped to its relying-party identifier
options.explanation: Correct — The authenticator binds credentials and assertions to the relying party, so a different domain cannot request the same credential.

options.label: The browser sends the account password too
options.explanation: Incorrect — WebAuthn does not need to expose the account password to the relying party.

options.label: The credential is copied into every trusted cookie
options.explanation: Incorrect — Credentials remain controlled by the authenticator rather than copied into cookies.

options.label: DNS guarantees that lookalike domains cannot exist
options.explanation: Incorrect — DNS permits distinct lookalike names; relying-party scoping supplies the security boundary.

stem: What does the HttpOnly attribute protect on a session cookie?

options.label: It prevents the browser from sending the cookie cross-site
options.explanation: Incorrect — SameSite, not HttpOnly, controls much cross-site cookie attachment.

options.label: It prevents browser scripts from reading the cookie
options.explanation: Correct — HttpOnly removes the cookie from script-accessible APIs, reducing session theft through script execution.

options.label: It encrypts the cookie value in storage
options.explanation: Incorrect — HttpOnly is an access restriction, not encryption.

options.label: It limits the cookie to one URL path
options.explanation: Incorrect — The Path attribute controls path matching.

stem: What does the Secure attribute require for a session cookie?

options.label: The cookie value must be a signed JWT
options.explanation: Incorrect — Secure applies regardless of the cookie value format.

options.label: JavaScript cannot read the cookie
options.explanation: Incorrect — That restriction is supplied by HttpOnly.

options.label: The browser sends it only over secure transport
options.explanation: Correct — Secure restricts cookie transmission to HTTPS rather than plaintext HTTP.

options.label: The cookie is deleted when the tab closes
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cookie lifetime is controlled by expiry and browser session semantics.

sources.title: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: Which risk is the SameSite cookie attribute primarily intended to reduce?

options.label: Reading cookies through injected same-origin JavaScript
options.explanation: Incorrect — HttpOnly limits script access; SameSite does not neutralize same-origin XSS.

options.label: Offline guessing of password verifiers
options.explanation: Incorrect — Password hashing controls offline guessing.

options.label: Packet capture on an HTTP connection
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS and Secure cookies address transport exposure.

options.label: Automatic credential attachment on cross-site requests
options.explanation: Correct — SameSite limits when browsers attach cookies in cross-site contexts, reducing common CSRF paths.

stem: What property should a newly generated session identifier have?

options.label: Enough unpredictability to make guessing impractical
options.explanation: Correct — A session ID is a bearer secret, so it needs cryptographic randomness and sufficient entropy.

options.label: A visible user ID prefix for debugging
options.explanation: Incorrect — Predictable identity material helps attackers narrow guesses and leaks account information.

options.label: A timestamp as its only value
options.explanation: Incorrect — Timestamps are predictable and do not provide adequate entropy.

options.label: The same value on every device
options.explanation: Incorrect — Reusing one identifier broadens exposure and complicates revocation.

stem: When should an application replace a pre-authentication session identifier?

options.label: Only after the user changes their password
options.explanation: Incorrect — Waiting leaves the login transition vulnerable to session fixation.

options.label: Immediately after successful authentication
options.explanation: Correct — Renewing the identifier at a privilege transition prevents an attacker-fixed ID from becoming authenticated.

options.label: Whenever a static asset is requested
options.explanation: Incorrect — Static asset requests do not change authentication privilege.

options.label: After the identifier has appeared in logs
options.explanation: Incorrect — A logged secret should be treated as exposed, but this is not the normal fixation boundary.

sources.title: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A cookie-authenticated form changes an email address. What proves the request came through the application interaction rather than an attacker page?

options.label: The presence of the session cookie
options.explanation: Incorrect — The browser automatically sends the session cookie on many forged requests.

options.label: A hidden field containing the user ID
options.explanation: Incorrect — An attacker can copy or choose a non-secret identifier.

options.label: A server-validated anti-CSRF token
options.explanation: Correct — A secret or session-bound token unavailable to the attacker site lets the server distinguish the intended workflow.

options.label: A POST method instead of GET
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cross-site pages can submit POST forms, so the method alone is insufficient.

stem: Why must an API enforce authorization even when its CORS policy names only one frontend origin?

options.label: CORS encrypts requests only after authorization
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS encrypts transport; CORS does not.

options.label: CORS validates the user password at the edge
options.explanation: Incorrect — CORS processing has no password-verification role.

options.label: CORS makes all allowed origins same-origin
options.explanation: Incorrect — An allowed cross-origin read remains cross-origin and does not replace access control.

options.label: CORS governs browser response access, not server authorization
options.explanation: Correct — Non-browser clients and some cross-origin requests can still reach the API, so the server must authorize every operation.

sources.title: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A template inserts untrusted text into an HTML text node. What is the primary output defense?

options.label: Encode it for the HTML text context
options.explanation: Correct — Context-appropriate HTML entity encoding keeps data from becoming markup in a text node.

options.label: URL-encode the entire rendered page
options.explanation: Incorrect — URL encoding is for URL components and does not safely encode an HTML document.

options.label: Hash the input before displaying it
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hashing destroys the desired text and is not an output-context control.

options.label: Set the cookie SameSite attribute
options.explanation: Incorrect — SameSite affects cookie attachment, not HTML parsing.

stem: What role should Content Security Policy play in an XSS defense?

options.label: A replacement for contextual output encoding
options.explanation: Incorrect — CSP is not a substitute for fixing injection sinks and encoding data for its context.

options.label: A defense-in-depth restriction on executable resources
options.explanation: Correct — CSP can limit script execution and resource loading, but safe templating and encoding remain necessary.

options.label: A server-side SQL query validator
options.explanation: Incorrect — CSP is enforced by browsers and does not parse database queries.

options.label: A password hashing configuration
options.explanation: Incorrect — CSP has no role in password-verifier storage.

sources.title: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A malicious comment is saved and later executes in every viewer’s browser. What class of flaw is this?

options.label: Cross-site request forgery
options.explanation: Incorrect — CSRF induces an authenticated request but does not require a stored script payload.

options.label: Server-side request forgery
options.explanation: Incorrect — SSRF makes the server initiate a request; this payload executes in browsers.

options.label: Stored cross-site scripting
options.explanation: Correct — The payload persists in application storage and executes when other users render the stored content.

options.label: SQL transaction replay
options.explanation: Incorrect — The symptom concerns browser script execution, not replaying a database transaction.

sources.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: Why do parameterized SQL queries stop ordinary input from changing query structure?

options.label: The database encrypts every parameter automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect — Parameterization is a parsing boundary, not automatic encryption.

options.label: The driver grants parameters read-only privileges
options.explanation: Incorrect — Database privileges belong to the connection or role, not each bound value.

options.label: The query is hidden from database logs
options.explanation: Incorrect — Logging behavior is unrelated to whether input is parsed as syntax.

options.label: The driver keeps parameter values separate from SQL syntax
options.explanation: Correct — Bound parameters are treated as data instead of being reparsed as query operators.

stem: Where should a client avoid placing a long-lived API key because intermediaries commonly record it?

options.label: In the request URL
options.explanation: Correct — URLs are frequently retained in browser history, proxy logs, analytics, and referrer data.

options.label: In an authorization header over TLS
options.explanation: Incorrect — A header over TLS is the conventional transport location, though the server must still protect logs.

options.label: In a protected secret manager before use
options.explanation: Incorrect — A secret manager reduces unmanaged copies at rest.

options.label: In a short-lived process memory buffer
options.explanation: Incorrect — Necessary runtime use in memory is less exposed than placing the key in the URL.

stem: A build service only uploads artifacts to one repository. How should its API credential be scoped?

options.label: Grant organization-owner access for reliability
options.explanation: Incorrect — Owner access needlessly expands the credential blast radius.

options.label: Grant only upload access to that repository
options.explanation: Correct — Least privilege limits what a stolen build credential can change.

options.label: Reuse the production administrator key
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sharing a powerful key destroys workload isolation and attribution.

options.label: Allow every repository but restrict the key name
options.explanation: Incorrect — A descriptive name is not an authorization boundary.

stem: Which permission design follows least privilege for an invoice-reading worker?

options.label: Administrator access with audit logging enabled
options.explanation: Incorrect — Logs aid detection but do not reduce excessive authority.

options.label: Write access to all finance tables for future needs
options.explanation: Incorrect — Speculative permissions enlarge the impact of compromise.

options.label: Read access only to the invoices it processes
options.explanation: Correct — The worker receives the minimum operations and resource scope needed for its task.

options.label: A shared root credential rotated monthly
options.explanation: Incorrect — Rotation cannot compensate for unnecessary root authority or sharing.

stem: How should an authorization policy handle a request that matches no explicit rule?

options.label: Allow it for authenticated users
options.explanation: Incorrect — Authentication alone does not establish permission for the requested action.

options.label: Allow it when no error is logged
options.explanation: Incorrect — Logging state is not an authorization decision.

options.label: Ask the client to declare its role
options.explanation: Incorrect — Client-supplied role claims cannot be trusted without server validation.

options.label: Deny the request
options.explanation: Correct — Deny-by-default ensures missing or newly introduced cases do not silently gain access.

sources.title: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3

stem: What does a correctly authenticated TLS connection primarily provide to application traffic?

options.label: Confidentiality, integrity, and peer authentication
options.explanation: Correct — TLS protects bytes from observation or modification and authenticates the endpoint according to the selected mode.

options.label: Authorization to every application resource
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS authenticates a connection endpoint but application authorization remains separate.

options.label: Permanent protection after plaintext is logged
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS protects data in transit, not copies written by endpoints.

options.label: Guaranteed absence of application vulnerabilities
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS does not repair injection or access-control defects.

stem: A client trusts a certificate chain but the certificate names a different service. What must it do?

options.label: Accept because the issuing CA is trusted
options.explanation: Incorrect — A valid chain does not authorize the certificate for every hostname.

options.label: Reject the connection for identity mismatch
options.explanation: Correct — Chain trust is insufficient when the reference service identity does not match an authenticated certificate identifier.

options.label: Rewrite the request Host header to match
options.explanation: Incorrect — Changing application routing does not prove the intended service identity.

options.label: Disable certificate checks for this request
options.explanation: Incorrect — Disabling verification enables impersonation rather than resolving the mismatch.

stem: What threat does an HSTS policy reduce after a browser has learned it?

options.label: SQL injection in HTTPS requests
options.explanation: Incorrect — HSTS controls transport selection, not SQL construction.

options.label: Stolen credentials reused on another service
options.explanation: Incorrect — Credential reuse requires authentication controls, not an HTTPS-only policy.

options.label: Downgrade to plaintext HTTP for that host
options.explanation: Correct — The browser rewrites or blocks insecure navigation for an HSTS host during the policy lifetime.

options.label: Authorization bypass inside the application
options.explanation: Incorrect — HSTS does not decide which resources a user may access.

sources.title: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

stem: A download endpoint maps user names to files under one directory. What check is essential after path resolution?

options.label: The original text contains a file extension
options.explanation: Incorrect — An extension does not prove where the resolved path points.

options.label: The request uses an authenticated session
options.explanation: Incorrect — An authenticated user can still submit a traversal path outside their authorized directory.

options.label: The response has a content type
options.explanation: Incorrect — Response metadata does not constrain filesystem lookup.

options.label: The resolved path remains inside the allowed root
options.explanation: Correct — Canonical resolution followed by a root-boundary check prevents parent traversal from escaping the intended directory.

sources.title: OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A service fetches status only from three known internal endpoints. What is the strongest first-line SSRF control?

options.label: Allowlist the exact permitted destinations
options.explanation: Correct — A narrow business requirement permits positive validation of the only hosts and ports the server should reach.

options.label: Block the string localhost
options.explanation: Incorrect — A denylist misses alternate names, encodings, and other internal addresses.

options.label: Require the supplied URL to use HTTPS
options.explanation: Incorrect — HTTPS can still target an attacker-controlled or internal service.

options.label: Hide fetch errors from the caller
options.explanation: Incorrect — Error suppression does not prevent the outbound request.

sources.title: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet

stem: A service needs to create a directory whose name is user-controlled. What design best avoids command injection?

options.label: Escape spaces and concatenate a command string
options.explanation: Incorrect — Other metacharacters and platform rules can still alter shell interpretation.

options.label: Call a filesystem API instead of a shell command
options.explanation: Correct — A dedicated library operation avoids placing input into a shell grammar at all.

options.label: Run the shell command as administrator
options.explanation: Incorrect — Higher privilege increases the impact of injection.

options.label: Base64-encode the command output
options.explanation: Incorrect — Output representation does not protect command construction.

stem: What server behavior makes logout effective for a stateful session?

options.label: Only hide authenticated controls in the page
options.explanation: Incorrect — A client-side visual change does not stop direct authenticated requests.

options.label: Rename the session cookie in JavaScript
options.explanation: Incorrect — Renaming one browser value does not revoke the server-recognized credential.

options.label: Invalidate the server-side session record
options.explanation: Correct — Deleting or revoking server state prevents reuse even if an old cookie value remains available.

options.label: Clear the browser history entry
options.explanation: Incorrect — History cleanup does not invalidate the session secret.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authenticator and Verifier Requirements

stem: Why should login failures avoid revealing whether the account or password was wrong?

options.label: To make password hashing faster
options.explanation: Incorrect — Response wording does not change verifier computation cost.

options.label: To prevent TLS certificate expiry
options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificate lifecycle is unrelated to authentication error messages.

options.label: To let clients skip rate limits
options.explanation: Incorrect — Uniform errors complement, rather than replace, abuse controls.

options.label: To reduce account enumeration
options.explanation: Correct — A uniform external response gives attackers less evidence about which identifiers are registered.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework

stem: What does verifying a downloaded dependency against a trusted digest detect?

options.label: Artifact bytes that differ from the expected release
options.explanation: Correct — A cryptographic digest comparison detects modification or substitution of the downloaded bytes.

options.label: Every vulnerability in the expected release
options.explanation: Incorrect — Integrity verification cannot establish that authentic source code is vulnerability-free.

options.label: Whether the maintainer used MFA
options.explanation: Incorrect — A digest says nothing about the maintainer authentication process.

options.label: Whether the dependency requests excessive runtime privileges
options.explanation: Incorrect — Runtime permission analysis is separate from artifact integrity.

stem: What should a threat-model data-flow diagram mark explicitly?

options.label: Only classes that contain cryptographic code
options.explanation: Incorrect — Threats also arise in storage, actors, processes, and non-cryptographic flows.

options.label: Trust boundaries where data changes control domains
options.explanation: Correct — Boundary crossings reveal where identity, validation, and privilege assumptions must be reassessed.

options.label: Every source-code line executed
options.explanation: Incorrect — A threat model abstracts relevant assets and flows rather than duplicating implementation.

options.label: Only failures already observed in production
options.explanation: Incorrect — Threat modeling anticipates plausible abuse before incidents occur.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authenticator and Verifier Requirements

stem: Why is password verification normally based on a salted password hash rather than reversible encryption?

options.label: Hashing guarantees users choose unique passwords
options.explanation: Incorrect — Users may choose the same password; salts separate the stored verifiers.

options.label: Encryption cannot protect any data at rest
options.explanation: Incorrect — Encryption is appropriate when plaintext recovery is a requirement.

options.label: The verifier need not recover the original password
options.explanation: Correct — One-way password hashing supports comparison while avoiding a decryption key that reveals every stored password.

options.label: Hashing prevents online credential phishing
options.explanation: Incorrect — A user can still disclose a password to an impostor verifier.

sources.title: RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange

stem: An attacker intercepts an OAuth authorization code issued to a public client using PKCE. What blocks redemption?

options.label: The code contains the user password
options.explanation: Incorrect — Authorization codes do not need to contain or reveal the resource-owner password.

options.label: The browser CORS policy rejects every token request
options.explanation: Incorrect — Token redemption security cannot depend on a browser-only response policy.

options.label: The redirect URI is hidden from the attacker
options.explanation: Incorrect — Redirect URIs are generally registered and visible; PKCE supplies the per-transaction secret.

options.label: The attacker lacks the matching code verifier
options.explanation: Correct — The token endpoint compares the verifier to the challenge bound to the authorization request.

sources.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

stem: What should an OAuth client verify with a transaction-bound state value on callback?

options.label: The response belongs to the browser session that initiated authorization
options.explanation: Correct — Binding state to the initiating user agent helps reject login CSRF and response injection.

options.label: The access token is valid for every resource server
options.explanation: Incorrect — Resource servers validate token audience and scope separately.

options.label: The authorization server supports password grants
options.explanation: Incorrect — State does not negotiate grant support.

options.label: The user approved every future scope
options.explanation: Incorrect — Consent applies to the requested authorization, not unlimited future scope.

sources.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

stem: Why should an authorization server compare redirect URIs exactly after client registration?

options.label: To make access tokens self-contained
options.explanation: Incorrect — Redirect validation does not determine token encoding.

options.label: To prevent codes from being sent to attacker-controlled destinations
options.explanation: Correct — Exact matching removes ambiguous or attacker-chosen redirect targets that can leak authorization responses.

options.label: To allow wildcard subdomains safely
options.explanation: Incorrect — Wildcards expand rather than constrain possible recipients.

options.label: To avoid validating the client identifier
options.explanation: Incorrect — Redirect validation supplements client identification; it does not replace it.

stem: Which token is intended to convey an OpenID Connect authentication result to the client?

options.label: The refresh token
options.explanation: Incorrect — A refresh token obtains new tokens and is not the authentication assertion consumed as the result.

options.label: The resource server access log
options.explanation: Incorrect — A log is operational evidence, not an OIDC protocol token.

options.label: The ID Token
options.explanation: Correct — OIDC defines the ID Token as a signed claim set about the end-user authentication event.

options.label: The PKCE code verifier
options.explanation: Incorrect — The verifier binds an authorization-code exchange but carries no identity claims.

stem: A client sent a nonce in its OpenID Connect authentication request. What must it check in the ID Token?

options.label: The subject claim equals the client secret
options.explanation: Incorrect — The subject identifies the end user, while the client secret is never an expected subject.

options.label: The issuer claim contains the redirect URI
options.explanation: Incorrect — Issuer identifies the authorization server, not the client callback.

options.label: The token has no expiration claim
options.explanation: Incorrect — Expiry is a security check, not a field to omit.

options.label: The nonce claim equals the value bound to that transaction
options.explanation: Correct — Matching the nonce links the returned token to the initiating request and helps detect replay.

sources.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

stem: What signal does refresh-token rotation provide when an invalidated old token is presented again?

options.label: Possible replay of a copied refresh token
options.explanation: Correct — Reusing a superseded token indicates that two parties may possess the same refresh-token lineage.

options.label: A harmless browser cache hit
options.explanation: Incorrect — Refresh tokens are protocol credentials, not cache validators.

options.label: Successful certificate pinning
options.explanation: Incorrect — Token rotation does not validate server certificates.

options.label: Proof that access scopes were reduced
options.explanation: Incorrect — Scope restriction is independent of reuse detection.

sources.title: RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

stem: An API receives a signed JWT access token whose audience names a different service. What should it do?

options.label: Accept it because the issuer is trusted
options.explanation: Incorrect — Issuer trust must be combined with audience and other claim validation.

options.label: Reject the token
options.explanation: Correct — A valid signature does not authorize use at a resource server outside the token audience.

options.label: Replace the audience locally
options.explanation: Incorrect — A resource server cannot rewrite signed authorization claims.

options.label: Forward it to every internal service
options.explanation: Incorrect — Bearer propagation broadens exposure and ignores audience restriction.

sources.title: RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

stem: How should a JWT verifier choose acceptable signature algorithms?

options.label: Accept any algorithm named by the token
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trusting the header can enable algorithm confusion or unsafe choices.

options.label: Try every installed algorithm until one succeeds
options.explanation: Incorrect — Algorithm probing expands the accepted verification surface.

options.label: Use a configured allowlist independent of the token header
options.explanation: Correct — The application must decide acceptable algorithms rather than letting attacker-controlled metadata select policy.

options.label: Skip verification when the token has an issuer
options.explanation: Incorrect — Claims are untrusted until cryptographic and semantic validation succeeds.

stem: What restriction is enforced by the __Host- prefix on a conforming cookie?

options.label: Readable only by service workers
options.explanation: Incorrect — The prefix does not grant a special script-access model.

options.label: Valid only for one browser tab
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cookie prefixes do not create tab-local storage.

options.label: Automatically encrypted by the browser
options.explanation: Incorrect — The prefix constrains cookie attributes, not value encryption.

options.label: Secure, host-only, and Path set to /
options.explanation: Correct — The prefix forbids Domain, requires Secure, and requires a root path, strengthening host scoping.

stem: A cross-origin fetch includes credentials. Why can the server not use * as Access-Control-Allow-Origin for the readable response?

options.label: Credentialed CORS requires an explicit matching origin
options.explanation: Correct — The Fetch CORS protocol does not allow the wildcard origin to authorize credentialed response sharing.

options.label: Wildcard origins disable TLS
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS negotiation is independent of the response header value.

options.label: The wildcard changes POST into GET
options.explanation: Incorrect — CORS headers do not rewrite the HTTP method.

options.label: The wildcard removes cookies from server logs
options.explanation: Incorrect — It neither controls logging nor retroactively removes credentials.

stem: What property must a CSP script nonce have on each protected response?

options.label: It equals the authenticated user ID
options.explanation: Incorrect — User IDs are predictable and can leak identity into policy.

options.label: It is unpredictable and freshly generated for that response
options.explanation: Correct — A reusable or guessable nonce lets an attacker mark injected script as authorized.

options.label: It remains constant across all deployments
options.explanation: Incorrect — A stable nonce ceases to distinguish server-approved script from injected script.

options.label: It is sent only in a cookie
options.explanation: Incorrect — The browser needs the nonce in policy and matching script elements.

stem: What does enforcing Trusted Types for script sinks change in a browser application?

options.label: Every network response becomes same-origin
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trusted Types governs DOM injection sinks, not the browser origin model.

options.label: All third-party JavaScript is cryptographically signed
options.explanation: Incorrect — The mechanism constrains values reaching sinks; it does not sign scripts.

options.label: Sensitive DOM sinks require values produced by approved policies
options.explanation: Correct — Enforcement replaces ordinary strings at injection sinks with typed values created through named reviewable policies.

options.label: Cookies become inaccessible to scripts
options.explanation: Incorrect — HttpOnly controls cookie access.

sources.title: OWASP DOM based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A page must insert untrusted text into an element without HTML formatting. Which DOM API is the safer fit?

options.label: innerHTML
options.explanation: Incorrect — innerHTML invokes the HTML parser and can turn attacker input into executable markup.

options.label: document.write
options.explanation: Incorrect — document.write parses HTML into the document and is a dangerous injection sink.

options.label: eval
options.explanation: Incorrect — eval treats a string as code and is unrelated to safe text insertion.

options.label: textContent
options.explanation: Correct — textContent creates text rather than parsing the value as HTML markup.

sources.title: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: Why should a synchronizer CSRF token be bound to the user session?

options.label: A token copied from another session should not authorize this one
options.explanation: Correct — Session binding prevents an attacker from supplying a valid token obtained under a different context.

options.label: The token can replace authentication
options.explanation: Incorrect — A CSRF token proves request provenance, not user identity.

options.label: The browser can use it as a TLS certificate
options.explanation: Incorrect — CSRF tokens do not participate in TLS authentication.

options.label: The database can skip authorization checks
options.explanation: Incorrect — Authorization remains required after CSRF validation.

sources.title: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: Why can SameSite=Lax be insufficient for an application that changes state on top-level GET requests?

options.label: Lax cookies are always readable by attacker scripts
options.explanation: Incorrect — Script readability depends on origin and HttpOnly, not Lax alone.

options.label: Lax cookies can accompany some top-level cross-site navigations
options.explanation: Correct — Lax permits cookies on qualifying top-level safe-method navigations, so unsafe GET semantics reintroduce CSRF risk.

options.label: Lax disables HTTPS certificate validation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cookie SameSite handling does not affect TLS.

options.label: Lax forces every request to use OPTIONS
options.explanation: Incorrect — It does not rewrite methods or require preflight for same-origin navigation.

sources.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A report lets users select a sort column, which cannot be represented by a bound value. What is the safe design?

options.label: Concatenate the raw column after escaping quotes
options.explanation: Incorrect — Identifier grammar is not safely controlled by string quote escaping.

options.label: Bind the column name as a string parameter
options.explanation: Incorrect — A value parameter becomes a literal value, not an SQL identifier.

options.label: Map an allowed client choice to a fixed column identifier
options.explanation: Correct — Allowlisting known identifiers avoids concatenating arbitrary syntax where parameters cannot stand for identifiers.

options.label: Grant the database account schema-owner rights
options.explanation: Incorrect — Extra privilege increases impact and does not make query construction safe.

sources.title: OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: An outbound URL passes validation, then responds with a redirect. What must the fetcher do before following it?

options.label: Trust it because the first host was allowed
options.explanation: Incorrect — An allowed host can redirect to a disallowed internal or alternate-scheme target.

options.label: Copy internal authorization headers to the new host
options.explanation: Incorrect — Forwarding credentials across destinations increases the compromise.

options.label: Disable TLS verification on the redirected request
options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificate verification remains necessary and is not an SSRF control.

options.label: Validate the new destination under the same SSRF policy
options.explanation: Correct — Redirects create another attacker-influenced hop that can target a blocked address.

sources.title: OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A URL hostname is allowed only when it resolves to public IP space. What must remain consistent at connection time?

options.label: The connected address is one that passed validation
options.explanation: Correct — Binding validation to the actual destination prevents DNS changes from redirecting the connection to private space.

options.label: The textual hostname contains a dot
options.explanation: Incorrect — Public-looking syntax says nothing about the resolved destination.

options.label: The response content type is JSON
options.explanation: Incorrect — A private service can also return JSON; the outbound target is the security boundary.

options.label: The request has a common browser user agent
options.explanation: Incorrect — User-agent text does not constrain routing.

sources.title: OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: Why should a general-purpose URL fetcher be unable to reach cloud instance-metadata addresses?

options.label: Metadata responses are always too large
options.explanation: Incorrect — Response size is not the primary security concern.

options.label: Metadata may expose workload identity credentials
options.explanation: Correct — SSRF access to metadata services can disclose short-lived cloud credentials or sensitive instance data.

options.label: Metadata servers cannot use HTTP
options.explanation: Incorrect — Many metadata services intentionally expose link-local HTTP endpoints.

options.label: Cloud providers require browser CORS approval
options.explanation: Incorrect — Server-side fetches are not protected by browser CORS.

sources.title: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

stem: A privileged file service validates a path, then opens it later. What can make that check insufficient?

options.label: The filename has only lowercase letters
options.explanation: Incorrect — Character restrictions do not stop filesystem objects from being replaced.

options.label: The response uses chunked transfer encoding
options.explanation: Incorrect — HTTP framing does not affect filesystem resolution.

options.label: A symlink can change between validation and use
options.explanation: Correct — A time-of-check/time-of-use race can redirect the later open outside the validated tree.

options.label: The process logs the canonical path
options.explanation: Incorrect — Logging evidence does not make the later lookup atomic.

sources.title: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

stem: Before extracting an archive entry, what should the service verify about its destination?

options.label: Its compressed size is an even number
options.explanation: Incorrect — Parity has no relationship to traversal safety.

options.label: Its extension appears in the archive name
options.explanation: Incorrect — A plausible extension does not constrain the resolved path.

options.label: Its timestamp is newer than the archive
options.explanation: Incorrect — Timestamps do not establish destination containment.

options.label: Its normalized destination stays under the extraction root
options.explanation: Correct — Archive names can contain parent segments or absolute paths that otherwise overwrite files outside the target directory.

stem: A service accepts untrusted messages. Which design reduces unsafe deserialization risk?

options.label: Use a simple data format with an explicit schema and allowed types
options.explanation: Correct — A constrained schema avoids reconstructing arbitrary runtime object graphs or invoking gadget behavior.

options.label: Deserialize native objects and inspect them afterward
options.explanation: Incorrect — Dangerous constructors or hooks may run before post-deserialization inspection.

options.label: Allow the sender to choose any class name
options.explanation: Incorrect — Attacker-controlled type selection expands the gadget surface.

options.label: Encrypt the serialized bytes with a public key
options.explanation: Incorrect — Confidentiality does not make an attacker-created object graph safe to instantiate.

stem: An account-update endpoint binds every JSON field directly to a user model. What prevents clients from setting admin-only properties?

options.label: Hide the admin field in the frontend form
options.explanation: Incorrect — A client can send fields that the UI does not display.

options.label: Allowlist fields writable through that endpoint
options.explanation: Correct — Explicit input models prevent unexpected privileged attributes from being assigned.

options.label: Rename the admin database column
options.explanation: Incorrect — Attackers can discover or guess fields; obscurity is not an assignment policy.

options.label: Return HTTP 202 for all updates
options.explanation: Incorrect — Response status does not constrain which fields are bound.

stem: A user changes /invoices/123 to /invoices/124. What server check prevents cross-account access?

options.label: Verify that 124 is a valid integer
options.explanation: Incorrect — Type validation does not establish ownership or permission.

options.label: Require the request to originate from the dashboard
options.explanation: Incorrect — Originating UI does not prove authorization to the object.

options.label: Authorize that user for the requested invoice object
options.explanation: Correct — Object-level authorization must be evaluated for the concrete resource on every request.

options.label: Use a longer numeric identifier
options.explanation: Incorrect — Harder guessing may reduce discovery but cannot replace access control.

stem: An admin endpoint is absent from the normal user interface. What still protects it from direct requests?

options.label: Minified frontend route names
options.explanation: Incorrect — Client code and traffic can reveal routes, and obscurity grants no permission.

options.label: A robots.txt disallow rule
options.explanation: Incorrect — Robots directives are voluntary crawler hints, not access controls.

options.label: A confirmation dialog in JavaScript
options.explanation: Incorrect — Attackers can bypass client-side interactions and call the endpoint directly.

options.label: Server-side function-level authorization
options.explanation: Correct — The handler must independently verify permission because clients can call undisplayed routes.

stem: A multitenant query loads a project by project ID alone. What additional predicate belongs in the authorization boundary?

options.label: The authenticated tenant identifier
options.explanation: Correct — Scoping the lookup to both tenant and object prevents identifiers from crossing tenant boundaries.

options.label: The browser window dimensions
options.explanation: Incorrect — Display information has no authorization meaning.

options.label: The project creation timestamp
options.explanation: Incorrect — A timestamp does not prove tenant ownership.

options.label: The API version header
options.explanation: Incorrect — Version negotiation does not establish resource access.

stem: A service only needs to compare presented opaque API keys. How can it reduce damage from a credential-table leak?

options.label: Store keys in URL query strings
options.explanation: Incorrect — URLs create additional plaintext copies in logs and histories.

options.label: Store a keyed or one-way verifier instead of recoverable key plaintext
options.explanation: Correct — Comparison can use a protected verifier without retaining the original bearer secret.

options.label: Use the same key for every customer
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sharing a bearer secret increases blast radius and removes attribution.

options.label: Embed keys in public client JavaScript
options.explanation: Incorrect — A shipped client secret is available to every user.

stem: Why is a managed secret store preferable to committing a production key in source control?

options.label: It makes the key safe to print in logs
options.explanation: Incorrect — Retrieved secrets must still be redacted from logs.

options.label: It removes the need for workload authentication
options.explanation: Incorrect — The workload still needs an authenticated, authorized way to retrieve the secret.

options.label: It centralizes access policy, audit, and rotation without source history copies
options.explanation: Correct — A secret store limits retrieval and supports lifecycle controls while repositories retain every committed revision.

options.label: It guarantees the consuming process cannot be compromised
options.explanation: Incorrect — A compromised authorized process may still misuse a secret it can access.

stem: How can an API rotate signing keys without rejecting all tokens issued just before the change?

options.label: Accept unsigned tokens during deployment
options.explanation: Incorrect — Removing authentication creates a critical bypass.

options.label: Reuse one key identifier for unrelated key material
options.explanation: Incorrect — Ambiguous identifiers can make verification nondeterministic or unsafe.

options.label: Extend every existing token indefinitely
options.explanation: Incorrect — Longer validity increases exposure and defeats bounded rotation.

options.label: Publish old and new verification keys for a bounded overlap
options.explanation: Correct — Overlapping verification lets existing short-lived tokens expire while new tokens use the new signer.

sources.title: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3

stem: What does mutual TLS add beyond ordinary server-authenticated TLS?

options.label: The server also verifies a client certificate during the handshake
options.explanation: Correct — mTLS authenticates both connection endpoints at the TLS layer.

options.label: The client no longer validates the server certificate
options.explanation: Incorrect — Mutual authentication retains server verification.

options.label: Every application user is automatically authorized
options.explanation: Incorrect — A workload certificate may identify a client, but application authorization still maps identity to permissions.

options.label: The connection becomes immune to endpoint compromise
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS cannot protect plaintext handled by a compromised endpoint.

sources.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

stem: Why must certificate validation enforce basic constraints on an intermediate certificate?

options.label: Every intermediate must name the application URL
options.explanation: Incorrect — Service identity is normally checked on the leaf certificate.

options.label: Only a certificate authorized as a CA may issue subordinate certificates
options.explanation: Correct — Basic constraints prevent an ordinary end-entity certificate from acting as a certification authority.

options.label: The intermediate must contain the user password
options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificates do not carry account passwords.

options.label: All intermediates must use the same public key
options.explanation: Incorrect — A chain consists of distinct issuers and subjects with their own keys.

sources.title: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3

stem: What benefit do ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchanges provide in TLS?

options.label: The server certificate never needs validation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Ephemeral exchange still requires authenticated negotiation.

options.label: Application messages remain secret after endpoint logging
options.explanation: Incorrect — Forward secrecy protects captured network traffic, not plaintext retained by endpoints.

options.label: Later server-key compromise does not reveal recorded session keys
options.explanation: Correct — Fresh ephemeral secrets keep past traffic keys from being derived solely from a later-stolen long-term key.

options.label: Clients can reuse one traffic key forever
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS derives per-connection traffic secrets rather than encouraging permanent reuse.

stem: What is the operational advantage of envelope encryption for many stored objects?

options.label: Every object must be decrypted with a public hash
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hashes are not decryption keys.

options.label: One plaintext data key is embedded in all objects
options.explanation: Incorrect — Reusing and exposing a plaintext key defeats separation.

options.label: Encryption removes the need to authorize object reads
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cryptography complements rather than replaces access control.

options.label: A key-encryption key can protect separately generated data keys
options.explanation: Correct — Objects use individual data keys while a centrally controlled key wraps those keys for policy and rotation.

stem: What invariant is critical when using AES-GCM with a fixed key?

options.label: Do not repeat a nonce with that key
options.explanation: Correct — GCM nonce reuse can expose plaintext relationships and undermine authentication.

options.label: Choose a nonce that is always secret
options.explanation: Incorrect — GCM requires uniqueness; secrecy is not the primary nonce requirement.

options.label: Use the same nonce to make retries deterministic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Deterministic reuse under one key is exactly the dangerous condition.

options.label: Derive the key from the ciphertext
options.explanation: Incorrect — The receiver needs an independently managed key before it can authenticate or decrypt.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authenticator and Verifier Requirements

stem: Where should an optional keyed password-hashing secret be kept relative to the verifier database?

options.label: In the same row beside each password hash
options.explanation: Incorrect — A database leak would then disclose both the verifier and the supposed extra secret.

options.label: In a separately protected secrets boundary
options.explanation: Correct — Separating the keyed secret from stored verifiers means a database-only theft lacks an input needed for checking guesses.

options.label: As a public constant in client JavaScript
options.explanation: Incorrect — A public constant supplies no additional secret.

options.label: Inside the user-visible salt field
options.explanation: Incorrect — Salts are intentionally stored with verifiers and are not secret.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Authenticator and Verifier Requirements

stem: What control directly limits high-volume online credential guessing against one account?

options.label: Shorten every password to eight characters
options.explanation: Incorrect — Shorter passwords reduce guessing resistance.

options.label: Return detailed failure reasons
options.explanation: Incorrect — Detailed differences can enable enumeration and do not limit attempts.

options.label: Rate-limit or throttle failed authentication attempts
options.explanation: Correct — Online attempt controls raise attacker cost and bound repeated guesses at the verifier.

options.label: Disable TLS session resumption
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS resumption is not an authentication-attempt control.

stem: An attacker supplies a victim with a session ID, then the victim logs in without the ID changing. What vulnerability is present?

options.label: Certificate transparency failure
options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificate logging is unrelated to application session identifiers.

options.label: DNS rebinding
options.explanation: Incorrect — DNS rebinding changes address resolution rather than fixing a session token.

options.label: Password-salt collision
options.explanation: Incorrect — Password verifier salts do not control session identity.

options.label: Session fixation
options.explanation: Correct — The attacker-chosen identifier becomes associated with the authenticated session and can be reused.

stem: Why might an application require reauthentication before changing registered authenticators?

options.label: An old session alone may be insufficient for a high-impact account change
options.explanation: Correct — Fresh authentication reduces damage from an unattended or stolen long-lived session.

options.label: Reauthentication changes the TLS cipher suite
options.explanation: Incorrect — Application authentication does not renegotiate TLS cryptography.

options.label: It makes authorization checks unnecessary
options.explanation: Incorrect — The action still requires authorization after identity is refreshed.

options.label: It converts a bearer session into a database lock
options.explanation: Incorrect — Session freshness and database concurrency are unrelated.

stem: What boundary does a seccomp filter enforce for a Linux process?

options.label: Which HTTP origins may read its responses
options.explanation: Incorrect — Browser CORS governs cross-origin reads, not process syscalls.

options.label: Which system calls and arguments the process may invoke
options.explanation: Correct — Seccomp BPF filters kernel entry points according to a configured syscall policy.

options.label: Which SQL rows the process may query
options.explanation: Incorrect — Database authorization is outside the kernel syscall filter.

options.label: Which certificate authorities a browser trusts
options.explanation: Incorrect — Trust stores are not configured by seccomp.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

stem: Why should a team avoid treating a default container as equivalent to a virtual machine security boundary?

options.label: Containers cannot have filesystems
options.explanation: Incorrect — Containers commonly have layered filesystems and mounted volumes.

options.label: Virtual machines never need patching
options.explanation: Incorrect — Guest and hypervisor software still require security maintenance.

options.label: Containers share the host kernel and depend on layered isolation controls
options.explanation: Correct — Namespaces and cgroups isolate resources, but kernel attack surface and configuration remain shared concerns.

options.label: Containers always run without privileges
options.explanation: Incorrect — Container processes can be misconfigured with broad capabilities or host access.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

stem: Why drop Linux capabilities that a containerized process does not need?

options.label: To make the image digest shorter
options.explanation: Incorrect — Runtime privilege does not affect digest length.

options.label: To prevent all outbound network traffic automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect — Network policy is separate from most capability removal.

options.label: To cause the process to bypass file permissions
options.explanation: Incorrect — Dropping privilege strengthens rather than bypasses access checks.

options.label: To reduce privileged kernel operations available after compromise
options.explanation: Correct — Capabilities divide root powers; removing unused ones narrows what exploited code can ask the kernel to do.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

stem: What does a read-only container root filesystem primarily limit?

options.label: Persistent modification of packaged files by the running process
options.explanation: Correct — An exploited process cannot rewrite the immutable root layers, though explicitly writable mounts still need control.

options.label: Reading secrets from environment variables
options.explanation: Incorrect — Filesystem mutability does not hide process environment values.

options.label: Network calls to internal services
options.explanation: Incorrect — Egress controls are separate from filesystem mode.

options.label: CPU denial of service
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU limits and scheduling, not read-only storage, address compute exhaustion.

stem: Why does signing a serialized native-object payload not by itself make deserialization safe?

options.label: Signatures always reveal the private signing key
options.explanation: Incorrect — Correct signature verification does not disclose the private key.

options.label: A legitimately signed payload can still select dangerous object behavior
options.explanation: Correct — Authenticity proves who produced bytes, not that reconstructing their object graph has no gadgets or unsafe hooks.

options.label: Signed payloads cannot be schema-validated
options.explanation: Incorrect — Signatures and schema validation can coexist.

options.label: Serialization formats cannot carry signatures
options.explanation: Incorrect — Payloads can be signed externally or in an envelope.

sources.title: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet

stem: A process API bypasses the shell but appends an untrusted value as a command-line argument. What risk can remain?

options.label: The kernel treats every argument as executable shell code
options.explanation: Incorrect — Without a shell, the kernel passes argument strings to the program.

options.label: TLS will silently encrypt the argument
options.explanation: Incorrect — Transport security does not constrain local process arguments.

options.label: The value may be interpreted as a dangerous option by the target program
options.explanation: Correct — Avoiding shell metacharacters stops shell injection, but the invoked program still parses its own argument grammar.

options.label: The filesystem automatically rejects user-controlled names
options.explanation: Incorrect — Filesystem and program semantics still require validation.

sources.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

stem: A client supports several authorization servers. Which validation helps prevent an authorization response from one issuer being handled as if it came from another?

options.label: Use the same client secret at every issuer
options.explanation: Incorrect — Shared secrets increase coupling and do not identify which issuer produced a response.

options.label: Accept any token that contains the right email
options.explanation: Incorrect — An untrusted issuer can assert the same email value.

options.label: Choose the issuer from an unsigned token claim
options.explanation: Incorrect — Attacker-controlled response data cannot establish its own trust anchor.

options.label: Bind the transaction and response to the expected issuer
options.explanation: Correct — Issuer-aware state and response validation prevent a mix-up across authorization-server trust relationships.

sources.title: RFC 9449: OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession

stem: What does a DPoP-bound access token require from its presenter that a bearer token does not?

options.label: A proof signed with the bound private key for the request
options.explanation: Correct — Sender-constrained tokens require demonstrating possession of key material associated with the token.

options.label: The resource owner’s plaintext password
options.explanation: Incorrect — Token presentation should not disclose the user password.

options.label: A wildcard redirect URI
options.explanation: Incorrect — Redirect configuration is unrelated to proof at the resource server.

options.label: The authorization server’s private signing key
options.explanation: Incorrect — Clients never receive the issuer private key.

sources.title: RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

stem: Two applications accept JWTs from the same issuer for different purposes. What prevents a token from one context being reused in the other?

options.label: A shared parser with no claim checks
options.explanation: Incorrect — Syntax parsing alone cannot distinguish security contexts.

options.label: Mutually exclusive validation rules including audience and token type
options.explanation: Correct — Explicit typing and context-specific claims prevent a valid token from being confused with another JWT class.

options.label: Longer Base64URL segments
options.explanation: Incorrect — Encoding length does not establish intended use.

options.label: Using identical keys and accepted claims everywhere
options.explanation: Incorrect — Identical rules make cross-context substitution easier.

sources.title: RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

stem: Why should a JWT verifier not fetch a key from an arbitrary jku URL supplied in the token header?

options.label: It makes the JWT too short to verify
options.explanation: Incorrect — Header URLs increase rather than reduce token length.

options.label: It prevents tokens from carrying an audience
options.explanation: Incorrect — Audience claims are independent of key discovery metadata.

options.label: It lets untrusted metadata choose a network destination and trust source
options.explanation: Correct — An attacker can combine SSRF with attacker-controlled keys unless key locations are configured and constrained.

options.label: It forces the verifier to use symmetric cryptography
options.explanation: Incorrect — A jku value does not inherently select a symmetric algorithm.

stem: What can X.509 name constraints on an intermediate CA restrict?

options.label: The application roles assigned after TLS
options.explanation: Incorrect — Application authorization is outside certificate path name constraints.

options.label: The maximum HTTP response size
options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificate validation does not govern payload size.

options.label: The password length at the relying service
options.explanation: Incorrect — Password policy is unrelated to CA namespace delegation.

options.label: The namespace in which subordinate certificates may assert identities
options.explanation: Correct — Name constraints limit permitted or excluded names beneath that CA, reducing its delegated authority.

sources.title: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3

stem: Why should a server avoid processing non-idempotent actions from TLS 1.3 early data without an application replay defense?

options.label: 0-RTT data can be replayed across accepted connections
options.explanation: Correct — TLS 1.3 does not provide inherent replay protection for early application data.

options.label: Early data is always sent without encryption
options.explanation: Incorrect — 0-RTT data is encrypted, but replay remains a concern.

options.label: Certificates cannot be used with session resumption
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS resumption still authenticates according to its handshake design.

options.label: 0-RTT changes every request method to GET
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS transports bytes and does not rewrite HTTP methods.

sources.title: CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests

stem: What creates the core risk in HTTP request smuggling through a proxy chain?

options.label: Every component agrees on one strict parser
options.explanation: Incorrect — Consistent framing interpretation removes the parser differential needed for smuggling.

options.label: Components disagree about where one request ends and the next begins
options.explanation: Correct — Inconsistent parsing of framing fields lets attacker-controlled bytes be assigned to different requests by different hops.

options.label: The response uses a strong Content-Security-Policy
options.explanation: Incorrect — CSP controls browser resource execution, not HTTP message boundaries between servers.

options.label: The client validates the server certificate
options.explanation: Incorrect — TLS identity does not reconcile conflicting HTTP parsers behind the endpoint.

sources.title: OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: Why should URL validation and the outbound client use one canonical parser and representation?

options.label: Canonical parsing guarantees every destination is trustworthy
options.explanation: Incorrect — Parsing consistency still needs an allowlist and address policy.

options.label: Multiple parsers make TLS keys longer
options.explanation: Incorrect — URL parsing does not determine cryptographic key length.

options.label: Different parsers may disagree about the effective host or scheme
options.explanation: Correct — Parser differentials can make validation approve one destination while the connector reaches another.

options.label: The outbound client cannot follow redirects
options.explanation: Incorrect — Redirect behavior is independent and must be controlled separately.

sources.title: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

stem: Why should a file-access policy compare paths only after applying the same decoding and normalization used for lookup?

options.label: Normalization encrypts the filename
options.explanation: Incorrect — Normalization creates a consistent representation; it does not provide confidentiality.

options.label: Raw paths never contain separators
options.explanation: Incorrect — User-controlled paths can contain literal or encoded separators.

options.label: The filesystem ignores all Unicode characters
options.explanation: Incorrect — Filesystems and libraries handle Unicode with platform-specific semantics.

options.label: Alternate encodings can otherwise bypass a textual boundary check
options.explanation: Correct — Security comparison must operate on the effective path rather than an attacker-controlled representation.

stem: Why can an allowlist of top-level serialized classes still be insufficient in an object deserializer?

options.label: Allowed roots may reference nested gadget classes during graph reconstruction
options.explanation: Correct — Validation must cover the reachable object graph and dangerous callbacks, not only the first declared type.

options.label: Top-level classes cannot contain fields
options.explanation: Incorrect — Object roots commonly reference nested objects and collections.

options.label: Gadgets require the payload to be plaintext
options.explanation: Incorrect — Encryption or transport format does not remove dangerous behavior after decryption.

options.label: Deserialization never invokes application code
options.explanation: Incorrect — Many runtimes support hooks, constructors, or methods that execute during reconstruction.

sources.title: OWASP Prototype Pollution Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A JavaScript merge utility recursively accepts __proto__ from untrusted input. What security property is at risk?

options.label: TLS traffic keys are immediately disclosed
options.explanation: Incorrect — Object prototype mutation does not directly reveal TLS secrets.

options.label: Inherited properties of unrelated objects can be modified
options.explanation: Correct — Prototype pollution changes shared prototype state, potentially altering authorization or code-flow assumptions.

options.label: The SQL parser disables parameter binding
options.explanation: Incorrect — JavaScript object inheritance is separate from database parsing.

options.label: The browser origin of the page changes
options.explanation: Incorrect — Prototype mutation does not rewrite the document origin.

stem: A server reuses one CSP nonce across every response. What is the main failure?

options.label: Browsers stop supporting HTTPS
options.explanation: Incorrect — Nonce reuse affects CSP authorization, not transport negotiation.

options.label: All stylesheets become same-origin
options.explanation: Incorrect — Script nonce reuse does not change resource origins.

options.label: Once learned, the nonce can authorize injected script on later responses
options.explanation: Correct — A nonce is an authorization token for script elements and must not remain reusable across responses.

options.label: The nonce becomes a password hash salt
options.explanation: Incorrect — CSP nonces and password salts serve unrelated purposes.

stem: What question can verified build provenance answer about a released artifact?

options.label: Whether its code contains no exploitable defect
options.explanation: Incorrect — Provenance establishes origin and process evidence, not vulnerability absence.

options.label: Whether every runtime user is authorized
options.explanation: Incorrect — Runtime authorization is outside build provenance.

options.label: Whether the artifact will meet latency targets
options.explanation: Incorrect — Performance requires separate measurement.

options.label: Which source and build process produced it
options.explanation: Correct — Provenance records verifiable information about inputs, builder, and build process for an artifact.

stem: What does a matching reproducible build fail to prove by itself?

options.label: That the selected source and build instructions were benign
options.explanation: Correct — Reproducibility can confirm correspondence, while malicious or vulnerable inputs can still reproduce perfectly.

options.label: That two builds produced identical bytes
options.explanation: Incorrect — That comparison is exactly what a reproducible-build check can establish.

options.label: That the build inputs were available
options.explanation: Incorrect — A rebuild necessarily consumes some identified inputs, though provenance quality is separate.

options.label: That cryptographic digests can be compared
options.explanation: Incorrect — Digest comparison is a standard way to compare outputs.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework

stem: An internal package name also exists on a public registry with a higher version. What control directly mitigates dependency confusion?

options.label: Allow package managers to choose any fastest mirror
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unconstrained source selection creates the confusion opportunity.

options.label: Pin the package namespace and source to the intended internal registry
options.explanation: Correct — Explicit source policy prevents resolution from substituting a public package with the same name.

options.label: Remove the lockfile during CI
options.explanation: Incorrect — Removing resolution evidence makes unexpected source changes easier.

options.label: Grant install scripts administrator access
options.explanation: Incorrect — Higher install privilege increases impact if substitution occurs.

sources.title: NTIA: The Minimum Elements for an SBOM

stem: What does an SBOM inventory not establish on its own?

options.label: Which components and versions are declared present
options.explanation: Incorrect — Component identification is the core value of an SBOM.

options.label: That transitive packages can be recorded
options.explanation: Incorrect — SBOM formats can include dependency relationships.

options.label: That each listed component is authentic and untampered
options.explanation: Correct — An inventory names components; signatures, digests, and provenance establish artifact integrity and origin.

options.label: That teams can search exposure after a disclosure
options.explanation: Incorrect — Inventory data supports impact queries when a component becomes vulnerable.

stem: Why must artifact-signature verification also enforce an expected signer identity?

options.label: Signer identity determines the artifact file size
options.explanation: Incorrect — Identity policy does not affect bytes or size.

options.label: Any certificate makes all repositories equivalent
