options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificates carry identity context that verifiers must constrain.

options.label: Identity checks make digest verification unnecessary
options.explanation: Incorrect — Signature verification covers a digest, so artifact binding remains essential.

options.label: A valid signature from an untrusted identity is not authorization to release
options.explanation: Correct — Cryptographic validity proves control of some signing identity; policy decides which identities may produce this artifact.

stem: Which property is required of an isolated hardened build environment?

options.label: One build cannot influence another build or obtain provenance signing secrets
options.explanation: Correct — SLSA build isolation separates concurrent and subsequent builds and keeps platform signing material outside user steps.

options.label: Every build shares a writable cache with no validation
options.explanation: Incorrect — An unprotected shared cache enables cross-build influence.

options.label: User build steps sign their own provenance with the platform key
options.explanation: Incorrect — Exposing the platform signing key lets a build forge evidence.

options.label: The environment persists arbitrary files for the next project
options.explanation: Incorrect — Persistence violates ephemeral cross-build isolation.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: OpenID Connect security hardening

stem: What security improvement comes from CI obtaining cloud credentials through workload OIDC federation?

options.label: Every pull request receives permanent administrator keys
options.explanation: Incorrect — Permanent broad credentials are the exposure federation is meant to avoid.

options.label: Jobs exchange bounded identity claims for short-lived cloud credentials
options.explanation: Correct — Federation avoids storing a long-lived cloud secret and lets policy bind access to repository and workflow claims.

options.label: The cloud trusts any unsigned repository name
options.explanation: Incorrect — The provider validates a signed OIDC token and configured claims.

options.label: OIDC encrypts all build artifacts automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect — Federation authenticates workloads; artifact encryption is separate.

stem: A threat model omits a background queue that carries user-controlled jobs into a privileged worker. Why is that omission serious?

options.label: Queues cannot carry untrusted data
options.explanation: Incorrect — Producers can enqueue malicious values unless controls prevent it.

options.label: Background workers never hold privileges
options.explanation: Incorrect — Workers often hold database, network, or cloud permissions.

options.label: It hides a trust-boundary crossing and asynchronous attack surface
options.explanation: Correct — The queue transports attacker-influenced data into a different privilege domain and needs explicit validation and authorization analysis.

options.label: Only synchronous calls belong in data-flow diagrams
options.explanation: Incorrect — Threat models should include every relevant data flow regardless of timing.

stem: Why should an application avoid using one AES-GCM key for unrelated tenants and data purposes indefinitely?

options.label: GCM cannot encrypt more than one byte per key
options.explanation: Incorrect — GCM supports many messages when nonce and usage bounds are respected.

options.label: Separate keys make nonce uniqueness irrelevant
options.explanation: Incorrect — Each key still requires compliant nonce management.

options.label: One global key automatically enforces tenant authorization
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cryptographic sharing erases rather than creates tenant boundaries.

options.label: Key separation and rotation limit cross-tenant and lifetime blast radius
options.explanation: Correct — Purpose- and tenant-scoped keys reduce how much data one compromise or misuse can affect.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

stem: Why does a syscall allowlist still need CPU, memory, process, and time limits for untrusted code?

options.label: Allowed operations can still exhaust resources
options.explanation: Correct — A sandbox may prevent forbidden syscalls while permitted computation or allocation causes denial of service.

options.label: Resource limits validate OAuth audiences
options.explanation: Incorrect — Token semantics are unrelated to process quotas.

options.label: Seccomp automatically provides unlimited fair scheduling
options.explanation: Incorrect — Seccomp filters syscalls but does not define comprehensive resource governance.

options.label: Memory limits prevent every data exfiltration path
options.explanation: Incorrect — Resource quotas do not replace network and filesystem isolation.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-190: Application Container Security Guide

stem: Why is mounting a host runtime socket into a container commonly equivalent to granting host-level control?

options.label: Unix sockets cannot carry authenticated requests
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sockets can support authentication, but possession may still grant a powerful local API.

options.label: The socket API can create privileged workloads and access host resources
options.explanation: Correct — Control of the container runtime often permits launching containers with mounts or privileges that cross the original boundary.

options.label: A mount automatically becomes read-only
options.explanation: Incorrect — Mount mode must be configured and does not remove powerful API operations.

options.label: The container gets a separate physical kernel
options.explanation: Incorrect — Containers continue to rely on the host kernel and runtime.

stem: An authorization service caches allow decisions. What must the cache key include to avoid privilege reuse across contexts?

options.label: Only the requested URL path
options.explanation: Incorrect — The same path may have different permissions for users, tenants, and methods.

options.label: Only whether the previous decision was allow
options.explanation: Incorrect — A result is not enough to identify the context in which it was valid.

options.label: All identity, resource, action, and policy-version inputs that affect the decision
options.explanation: Correct — Omitting a decision input can return an allow computed for another principal, object, action, or policy state.

options.label: The frontend component that sent the request
options.explanation: Incorrect — UI identity is not the server authorization context.

stem: A workload must authenticate to a secret manager without storing another long-lived bootstrap secret. What pattern addresses this secret-zero problem?

options.label: Commit the bootstrap secret in a private repository
options.explanation: Incorrect — Repository history and developer access still expose a long-lived credential.

options.label: Place the bootstrap secret in the container image label
options.explanation: Incorrect — Image metadata is not a protected secret boundary.

options.label: Use one organization-wide key in every workload
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sharing a root key maximizes blast radius and prevents workload attribution.

options.label: Use platform-issued workload identity with short-lived credentials
options.explanation: Correct — An attested runtime identity can obtain bounded credentials without embedding a permanent bootstrap key.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Algorithmic thinking and peak finding

stem: A measured routine takes about four times as long whenever input size doubles. Which growth rate best fits that evidence?

options.label: Quadratic time, Θ(n²)
options.explanation: Correct — For a quadratic term, replacing n with 2n multiplies the dominant work by four.

options.label: Linear time, Θ(n)
options.explanation: Incorrect — Linear work would roughly double, not quadruple, when the input doubles.

options.label: Logarithmic time, Θ(log n)
options.explanation: Incorrect — A logarithmic routine grows only by an additive constant under input doubling.

options.label: Constant time, Θ(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — Constant-time work should not systematically increase with input size.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Algorithmic thinking and peak finding

stem: A running-time expression is 7n² + 40n + 900. What is its asymptotic order?

options.label: Θ(n)
options.explanation: Incorrect — The linear term is eventually smaller than the quadratic term.

options.label: Θ(n²)
options.explanation: Correct — The n² term dominates the linear and constant terms as n grows.

options.label: Θ(n³)
options.explanation: Incorrect — No cubic term exists, so this overstates the growth rate.

options.label: Θ(900)
options.explanation: Incorrect — A constant contributes no input-dependent asymptotic growth.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Algorithmic thinking and peak finding

stem: A service must reserve enough CPU for any valid input of size n. Which complexity bound is most directly useful?

options.label: A best-case lower bound
options.explanation: Incorrect — The cheapest input cannot establish enough capacity for harder inputs.

options.label: A single production timing
options.explanation: Incorrect — One observation does not bound all valid inputs or larger sizes.

options.label: A worst-case upper bound
options.explanation: Correct — An upper bound covers the greatest work among valid inputs of that size.

options.label: The source file length
options.explanation: Incorrect — Source length is not a bound on input-dependent execution work.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Algorithmic thinking and peak finding

stem: Two implementations are both O(n), but one is consistently ten times faster at expected sizes. What is the sound conclusion?

options.label: They must take equal wall-clock time
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sharing an asymptotic class does not imply equal constants or instruction costs.

options.label: The faster one is O(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — A smaller constant does not change linear growth into constant growth.

options.label: The slower one is necessarily incorrect
options.explanation: Incorrect — Performance differences do not by themselves establish a correctness defect.

options.label: Big-O alone does not compare their constants
options.explanation: Correct — Asymptotic classes omit constant factors that can dominate at practical input sizes.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Algorithmic thinking and peak finding

stem: A lookup is described as O(n). What does that statement guarantee by itself?

options.label: Its growth has an asymptotic upper bound proportional to n
options.explanation: Correct — Big-O states an eventual upper bound; it need not be the tightest bound.

options.label: Every lookup examines exactly n items
options.explanation: Incorrect — Asymptotic notation does not specify an exact operation count.

options.label: Its best case is linear
options.explanation: Incorrect — An upper bound says nothing by itself about the best case.

options.label: It cannot also be O(n²)
options.explanation: Incorrect — A linear upper bound also satisfies looser polynomial upper bounds.

stem: Which precondition makes ordinary binary search valid?

options.label: The array has an even length
options.explanation: Incorrect — Binary search handles odd and even lengths.

options.label: The searched range is ordered by the comparison key
options.explanation: Correct — Discarding half is safe only when order locates all smaller and larger candidates.

options.label: Every value is unique
options.explanation: Incorrect — Duplicates affect which match is returned, not whether halving works.

options.label: The target is known to exist
options.explanation: Incorrect — A correct search can report absence without that promise.

stem: A binary search starts with 1,024 candidates. At most how many halvings are needed to reduce the range to one candidate?

options.explanation: Incorrect — That corresponds to a linear scan rather than repeated halving.
Incorrect — One halving leaves 512 candidates; it is not the full search depth.
Correct — Because 1,024 is 2¹⁰, ten halvings reduce it to one.
Incorrect — Thirty-two is unrelated to log₂(1,024).

stem: What does a lower-bound binary search return when a sorted array contains duplicate keys?

options.label: An arbitrary matching position
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is possible for basic search but does not satisfy lower-bound semantics.

options.label: The final matching position
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is an upper-edge variant, not lower-bound.

options.label: The number of matching elements
options.explanation: Incorrect — Counting duplicates requires both range boundaries or an additional scan.

options.label: The first position whose value is not less than the target
options.explanation: Correct — Lower-bound preserves an invariant that identifies the left edge of the equal range.

stem: Why is mid = low + (high - low) / 2 preferred to (low + high) / 2 with fixed-width integers?

options.label: It avoids overflowing the sum low + high
options.explanation: Correct — Subtracting first keeps the intermediate within the established index range.

options.label: It changes logarithmic time to constant time
options.explanation: Incorrect — Both midpoint formulas leave the number of iterations logarithmic.

options.label: It sorts the input during the search
options.explanation: Incorrect — Midpoint arithmetic does not reorder data.

options.label: It guarantees the target exists
options.explanation: Incorrect — Arithmetic safety has no bearing on membership.

stem: Python bisect finds an insertion point in O(log n). Why can inserting into a list still be O(n)?

options.label: The comparison function becomes recursive
options.explanation: Incorrect — Bisect comparisons are not made recursive by insertion.

options.label: Elements after the position must be shifted
options.explanation: Correct — Finding an index is logarithmic, but contiguous-list insertion moves a suffix.

options.label: Binary search rechecks every prior midpoint
options.explanation: Incorrect — The search itself still performs logarithmically many comparisons.

options.label: Sorted lists disable random access
options.explanation: Incorrect — Python lists retain constant-time indexed access.

stem: Under a well-distributed hash function and controlled load factor, what lookup cost is normally expected?

options.label: O(log n) worst-case and expected
options.explanation: Incorrect — A basic hash table is not a balanced search tree.

options.label: O(n²) expected time
options.explanation: Incorrect — That would require pathological repeated work, not normal bounded-load hashing.

options.label: O(1) expected time
options.explanation: Correct — Expected bucket occupancy remains bounded when hashing distributes keys and resizing controls load.

options.label: Exactly one comparison
options.explanation: Incorrect — Collisions can require more than one comparison even under good distribution.

stem: Two different keys produce the same hash-table index. What has occurred?

options.label: A data race
options.explanation: Incorrect — A race concerns unsynchronized concurrent accesses, not equal hash indices.

options.label: A stack overflow
options.explanation: Incorrect — Stack depth is unrelated to the hash result.

options.label: A stable sort
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sorting stability concerns equal-key order, not table placement.

options.label: A hash collision
options.explanation: Correct — A collision is precisely multiple distinct keys mapping to the same slot or bucket.

stem: Why do many hash tables resize before the number of entries greatly exceeds the number of buckets?

options.label: To keep collision chains or probe sequences short
options.explanation: Correct — A bounded load factor preserves the assumptions behind expected constant-time operations.

options.label: To make hashes cryptographically secret
options.explanation: Incorrect — Resizing changes capacity, not the secrecy of the hash function.

options.label: To preserve insertion order
options.explanation: Incorrect — Ordering behavior is a separate representation choice.

options.label: To eliminate key equality checks
options.explanation: Incorrect — Colliding candidates still require equality checks after resizing.

stem: What can make a chained hash-table lookup degrade to O(n)?

options.label: The table having unused buckets
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unused capacity usually reduces rather than causes long chains.

options.label: Many keys landing in one bucket
options.explanation: Correct — A lookup may scan a chain containing nearly all stored keys.

options.label: The key being stored once
options.explanation: Incorrect — Normal unique-key storage does not imply a linear scan.

options.label: The hash value fitting in a machine word
options.explanation: Incorrect — Machine-word hashes are standard and do not force worst-case clustering.

stem: Why is mutating fields used by a stored key’s hash dangerous?

options.label: It automatically duplicates the value
options.explanation: Incorrect — Mutation does not create another table entry.

options.label: It converts expected O(1) into O(log n)
options.explanation: Incorrect — The more immediate problem is broken lookup invariants, not a tree-like complexity.

options.label: The key may no longer be found in the bucket chosen at insertion
options.explanation: Correct — Lookup computes a new hash while the entry remains at its old location.

options.label: It forces every bucket to resize
options.explanation: Incorrect — Capacity changes are triggered by load policy, not one key mutation.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Models of computation and document distance

stem: A dynamic array doubles capacity when full. What is the amortized cost of append over a long sequence?

options.label: O(n) for every append
options.explanation: Incorrect — Only growth-triggering appends copy the existing elements.

options.label: O(log n) per append
options.explanation: Incorrect — Capacity doubling counts growth events, not the average work per operation.

options.label: O(n²) per append
options.explanation: Incorrect — Even a resizing append performs one linear copy, not quadratic work.

options.label: O(1) per append
options.explanation: Correct — Occasional linear copies are spread across many cheap appends between growth events.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Models of computation and document distance

stem: Which statement about a doubling-array append is accurate?

options.label: One append can be O(n) while the amortized cost is O(1)
options.explanation: Correct — The resize is expensive individually, but total copying over n appends is linear.

options.label: Every append is worst-case O(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — An append that reallocates and copies is linear in current length.

options.label: Amortized O(1) means no append ever pauses
options.explanation: Incorrect — Amortization bounds sequence cost, not individual latency.

options.label: Worst-case and amortized bounds must match
options.explanation: Incorrect — They intentionally answer different questions about an operation sequence.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Models of computation and document distance

stem: What does the aggregate method do in amortized analysis?

options.label: Measures only the cheapest operation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Ignoring expensive operations would invalidate the sequence bound.

options.label: Bounds total cost of a sequence and divides by its operation count
options.explanation: Correct — The sequence-level bound yields a per-operation amortized cost.

options.label: Assumes every operation has identical cost
options.explanation: Incorrect — Amortized analysis is useful precisely when costs vary.

options.label: Replaces proof with a runtime benchmark
options.explanation: Incorrect — It is a mathematical accounting argument, not an empirical measurement.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Models of computation and document distance

stem: Why is growing an array by one slot on every full append usually worse than multiplying its capacity?

options.label: It makes indexed reads logarithmic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Contiguous-array indexing remains constant time.

options.label: It prevents the array from storing duplicates
options.explanation: Incorrect — Capacity policy does not affect value uniqueness.

options.label: Repeated copies make n appends take Θ(n²) total work
options.explanation: Correct — Copying lengths 1 through n produces an arithmetic sum with quadratic growth.

options.label: Multiplicative growth uses no extra space
options.explanation: Incorrect — It deliberately reserves unused capacity to reduce copying.

sources.title: MIT 6.006 — Models of computation and document distance

stem: Why might amortized O(1) append still be unsuitable for a strict tail-latency path?

options.label: Amortized bounds apply only to recursive code
options.explanation: Incorrect — They apply to any operation sequence with uneven costs.

options.label: O(1) always means one CPU instruction
options.explanation: Incorrect — Constant asymptotic work can include many instructions and allocations.

options.label: Tail latency ignores individual operations
options.explanation: Incorrect — Tail metrics are specifically sensitive to rare slow operations.

options.label: A resize can make a particular append take O(n)
options.explanation: Correct — The average bound permits occasional expensive operations that can violate a per-request deadline.

stem: What role does a base case play in a recursive function?

options.label: It stops further recursive calls for a terminal input
options.explanation: Correct — Without a reachable terminating case, recursive descent continues until a resource limit is hit.

options.label: It memoizes every intermediate result
options.explanation: Incorrect — Memoization is optional caching, not the definition of a base case.

options.label: It makes all recursion tail-recursive
options.explanation: Incorrect — Tail position depends on what happens after the recursive call.

options.label: It proves constant space usage
options.explanation: Incorrect — Recursive calls usually consume stack frames unless optimized away.

stem: A function recursively follows a linked list with one frame per node and fails only on very long lists. What resource is most likely exhausted?

options.label: The hash-table load factor
options.explanation: Incorrect — No hash table is implicated by the recursive traversal.

options.label: The call stack
options.explanation: Correct — Each nested call retains a frame until the recursion unwinds.

options.label: The network connection pool
options.explanation: Incorrect — Local call depth does not consume network connections.

options.label: The binary-search invariant
options.explanation: Incorrect — The failure is resource depth, not an ordered-search error.

stem: A recursive traversal has O(n) call depth and O(1) local data per call. What auxiliary space does it use without tail-call elimination?

options.label: O(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — Per-frame constant space accumulates across linear depth.

options.label: O(log n)
options.explanation: Incorrect — Logarithmic space would require logarithmic maximum depth.

options.label: O(n)
options.explanation: Correct — There can be n simultaneously live stack frames.

options.label: O(n²)
options.explanation: Incorrect — Linear frames with constant local storage do not multiply into a quadratic total.

stem: A divide-and-conquer routine makes two half-size calls and does Θ(n) merge work. Which recurrence describes it?

options.label: T(n) = T(n-1) + Θ(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — That describes one nearly full-size recursive call, not two halves.

options.label: T(n) = Θ(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — It omits all recursive and merge work.

options.label: T(n) = nT(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — This does not express the level-by-level divide-and-conquer structure.

options.label: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)
options.explanation: Correct — The recurrence records both recursive subproblems plus the linear combine step.

stem: Converting depth-first recursion to an explicit stack usually changes which property?

options.label: Where pending work is stored, not its asymptotic amount
options.explanation: Correct — Both forms retain the frontier; one uses call frames and the other a programmer-managed structure.

options.label: It always changes O(n) time to O(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — The same nodes still need to be processed.

options.label: It removes the need for a termination condition
options.explanation: Incorrect — The loop still needs a condition that exhausts pending work.

options.label: It guarantees breadth-first order
options.explanation: Incorrect — A LIFO explicit stack preserves depth-first behavior.

stem: A function accepts integers from 1 through 100 inclusive. Which compact test set best targets boundary mistakes?

options.label: 25, 50, and 75
options.explanation: Incorrect — Interior points are less likely to reveal inclusive-versus-exclusive mistakes.

options.label: 0, 1, 100, and 101
options.explanation: Correct — It exercises both valid endpoints and the immediately adjacent invalid values.

options.label: Only 1 and 100
options.explanation: Incorrect — Endpoints alone do not verify rejection immediately outside the range.

options.label: Only 0 and 101
options.explanation: Incorrect — Outside values do not verify that the valid endpoints are accepted.

stem: Why should a collection-processing unit test often include an empty collection?

options.label: It proves the algorithm is asymptotically optimal
options.explanation: Incorrect — One test input cannot establish a growth-rate proof.

options.label: It replaces tests for non-empty data
options.explanation: Incorrect — Empty input covers one boundary, not normal behavior.

options.label: Empty input exercises a structural boundary and initialization assumptions
options.explanation: Correct — Loops, reductions, and first-element access frequently fail at length zero.

options.label: It guarantees no null values exist
options.explanation: Incorrect — Collection length and element nullability are separate concerns.

stem: A loop should process indices 0 through n-1. Which condition is appropriate?

options.label: i <= n
options.explanation: Incorrect — This performs one extra iteration at index n.

options.label: i < n-1
options.explanation: Incorrect — This stops before processing the final valid element.

options.label: i == n
options.explanation: Incorrect — Starting at zero, equality does not define the continuing range.

options.label: i < n
options.explanation: Correct — The strict comparison includes n-1 and stops before the invalid index n.

stem: What is the main benefit of parametrizing the same assertion over many input/output pairs?

options.label: It expands coverage without duplicating test logic
options.explanation: Correct — The invariant stays in one place while cases remain visible and independently reported.

options.label: It makes every case execute concurrently
options.explanation: Incorrect — Parametrization does not inherently choose a parallel execution policy.

options.label: It eliminates the need to name cases
options.explanation: Incorrect — Good parameter sets still benefit from readable identifiers.

options.label: It converts unit tests into benchmarks
options.explanation: Incorrect — Repeating assertions across cases does not measure performance.

stem: Which assertion failure is most useful when a parser mishandles one table-driven case?

options.label: A message saying only “false”
options.explanation: Incorrect — It gives no clue which case or value diverged.

options.label: One that identifies the input and expected versus actual result
options.explanation: Correct — Specific case context turns a failed assertion into actionable diagnostic evidence.

options.label: A complete dump of unrelated process state
options.explanation: Incorrect — Noise can obscure the relevant mismatch and expose sensitive data.

options.label: No message because failures are self-explanatory
options.explanation: Incorrect — Parameterized failures often need case identifiers to be understandable.

stem: What is BFS time complexity on an adjacency-list graph with V vertices and E edges?

options.label: O(VE)
options.explanation: Incorrect — BFS does not rescan every edge for every vertex.

options.label: O(log V)
options.explanation: Incorrect — Even discovering all vertices requires linear output-sensitive work.

options.label: O(V + E)
options.explanation: Correct — Each reachable vertex is enqueued once and each adjacency entry is examined a constant number of times.

options.label: O(E²)
options.explanation: Incorrect — Edges are not compared pairwise.

stem: Why can traversing an adjacency-matrix graph cost O(V²) even when it has few edges?

options.label: Matrix lookup is logarithmic
options.explanation: Incorrect — A matrix cell is directly indexed.

options.label: BFS duplicates every edge V times in memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — The scan cost arises from absent-edge cells, not duplicated edges.

options.label: Queue operations become quadratic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Normal BFS queue operations remain constant amortized time.

options.label: Discovering each vertex’s neighbors requires scanning an entire matrix row
options.explanation: Correct — The representation stores V possible neighbors per vertex whether or not edges exist.

stem: Why is ordinary Dijkstra’s algorithm invalid with negative-weight edges?

options.label: A vertex considered settled can later receive a shorter path
options.explanation: Correct — Negative edges break the greedy finality of the current minimum distance.

options.label: Negative weights cannot be represented numerically
options.explanation: Incorrect — Signed numeric types can represent them; the issue is the proof invariant.

options.label: The priority queue cannot store negative keys
options.explanation: Incorrect — Heaps compare negative values normally.

options.label: All negative edges form cycles
options.explanation: Incorrect — A graph can have a negative edge without a cycle.

stem: What does marking vertices visited prevent in BFS on a cyclic graph?

options.label: Edges from being traversed at all
options.explanation: Incorrect — BFS still examines incident edges to find undiscovered neighbors.

options.label: Repeated enqueueing and potentially unbounded revisits
options.explanation: Correct — The visited set ensures each vertex is discovered once despite back edges.

options.label: The queue from using memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — The frontier still consumes space.

options.label: The graph from containing self-loops
options.explanation: Incorrect — Visited state handles loops but does not alter the graph.

stem: For a very dense graph, why may an adjacency matrix be reasonable?

options.label: It makes shortest paths constant time
options.explanation: Incorrect — Representation alone does not solve shortest-path computation.

options.label: It stores only existing edges
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is an adjacency-list property, not a matrix property.

options.label: Its Θ(V²) space is close to the number of possible edges and edge lookup is O(1)
options.explanation: Correct — When E approaches V², the matrix overhead is proportional to actual density.

options.label: It removes the need for vertex identifiers
options.explanation: Incorrect — Rows and columns still correspond to vertices.

stem: What does a sampling CPU profiler primarily estimate?

options.label: The exact number of every function call
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sampling can miss short calls and is not an exact invocation counter.

options.label: Only heap allocation sizes
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU sampling targets execution location, not just allocation events.

options.label: The semantic correctness of each branch
options.explanation: Incorrect — Profiles measure behavior; they do not prove program correctness.

options.label: Where execution time is distributed by periodically observing stacks or instruction pointers
options.explanation: Correct — The share of samples approximates the share of on-CPU time spent in code regions.

stem: A profile contains mostly raw addresses instead of function names. What artifact is most directly missing or unavailable?

options.label: Usable symbol information
options.explanation: Correct — Symbols map sampled instruction addresses back to functions and source locations.

options.label: A larger test dataset
options.explanation: Incorrect — More inputs do not translate addresses into names.

options.label: A hash-table resize
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hash capacity is unrelated to symbolization.

options.label: An assertion message
options.explanation: Incorrect — Assertions report detected failures, not profiling addresses.

stem: Why can profiling only an unoptimized debug build mislead a production optimization effort?

options.label: Debug builds cannot execute loops
options.explanation: Incorrect — They run loops, usually with less optimization.

options.label: Compiler optimization changes inlining, code layout, and execution cost
options.explanation: Correct — The measured hot path may differ materially from the deployed binary.

options.label: Production builds contain no symbols at all
options.explanation: Incorrect — Symbols can be preserved separately or included without disabling optimization.

options.label: Sampling requires source code to be interpreted
options.explanation: Incorrect — Native profilers sample compiled execution.

stem: What does perf counter multiplexing mean when more hardware events are requested than counters can measure simultaneously?

options.label: Every event is counted twice
options.explanation: Incorrect — Multiplexing samples intervals rather than duplicating all events.

options.label: The CPU switches to interpreted execution
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hardware counter scheduling does not change the program’s execution mode.

options.label: Events are time-shared and counts are scaled from partial measurement
options.explanation: Correct — The kernel rotates event groups, reducing simultaneous observation time.

options.label: Counters are written into application variables
options.explanation: Incorrect — The performance subsystem maintains measurements outside normal program state.

stem: Before optimizing the hottest function in a profile, what should be verified first?

options.label: The function has the longest name
options.explanation: Incorrect — Names provide no evidence about user-visible cost.

options.label: Every source line has equal sample count
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hotspots inherently produce unequal sample distributions.

options.label: The profiler reports zero overhead
options.explanation: Incorrect — Some overhead is acceptable; representativeness is the essential validity check.

options.label: The workload and environment represent the performance problem users experience
options.explanation: Correct — A precise profile of an unrepresentative workload can optimize the wrong bottleneck.

stem: In a CPU flame graph, what does a frame’s horizontal width represent?

options.label: The frequency with which that function appears in sampled stacks
options.explanation: Correct — Wider frames account for a larger share of the captured on-CPU samples.

options.label: The function’s source-code line count
options.explanation: Incorrect — Frame width is sample frequency, not static code size.

options.label: The chronological duration of one call
options.explanation: Incorrect — The x-axis aggregates stacks and is not a left-to-right timeline.

options.label: The maximum heap bytes allocated by the function
options.explanation: Incorrect — A CPU flame graph is not an allocation profile.

stem: What does vertical position in a flame graph represent?

options.label: Wall-clock ordering from left to right
options.explanation: Incorrect — Flame graphs alphabetically aggregate stacks rather than showing time sequence.

options.label: Stack ancestry, with callees above callers
options.explanation: Correct — Frames are stacked according to the captured call chain.

options.label: Thread priority
options.explanation: Incorrect — Height reflects call depth, not scheduler priority.

options.label: Algorithmic complexity class
options.explanation: Incorrect — No axis directly encodes Big-O.

stem: A wide plateau has many narrow child frames above it. What is a reasonable first interpretation?

options.label: The parent is necessarily blocked on disk
options.explanation: Incorrect — A CPU flame graph alone does not establish off-CPU I/O waits.

options.label: Every child has equal execution cost
options.explanation: Incorrect — Different child widths show different sample shares.

options.label: The parent or its descendants account for substantial sampled time across several callees
options.explanation: Correct — The wide base aggregates time in the entire subtree rooted at that function.

options.label: The code below the plateau never executes
options.explanation: Incorrect — The plateau itself demonstrates sampled execution in that ancestry.

stem: What does a differential flame graph help compare?

options.label: Two source files for textual merge conflicts
options.explanation: Incorrect — It compares performance profiles, not version-control diffs.

options.label: Heap object reachability within one snapshot
options.explanation: Incorrect — That requires heap analysis rather than differential CPU stacks.

options.label: Only functions with identical addresses
options.explanation: Incorrect — Profiles can be symbolized and compared by stack identity.

options.label: Changes in stack sample frequency between two profiles
options.explanation: Correct — Color and width differences highlight where execution grew or shrank between runs.

stem: A native flame graph shows broken or truncated call stacks. Which build/runtime issue is a likely cause?

options.label: Unwind information or frame pointers are unavailable
options.explanation: Correct — Reliable stack walking needs frame pointers or suitable unwind metadata.

options.label: The input is already sorted
options.explanation: Incorrect — Input ordering cannot remove call-stack metadata.

options.label: The hash load factor is low
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hash distribution has no bearing on unwinding.

options.label: The test assertions are parametrized
options.explanation: Incorrect — Test organization does not determine stack reconstruction.

stem: What connects spans belonging to one distributed request?

options.label: A globally identical span identifier
options.explanation: Incorrect — Each span has its own span ID within the trace.

options.label: A shared trace identifier propagated across service boundaries
options.explanation: Correct — Trace context carries the trace ID so independently created spans can be correlated.

options.label: The same process identifier
options.explanation: Incorrect — A distributed request crosses processes and hosts.

options.label: A common source-code line number
options.explanation: Incorrect — Services need not share code or line layouts.

stem: What relationship normally represents service B handling an RPC initiated by a span in service A?

options.label: Both spans start unrelated traces
options.explanation: Incorrect — That loses end-to-end request correlation.

options.label: Both spans reuse the same span ID
options.explanation: Incorrect — Span IDs identify individual operations and must not be shared this way.

options.label: B’s server span is a child of the propagated A client span
options.explanation: Correct — Parent context captures causality across the request boundary.

options.label: B stores A’s stack trace as its name
options.explanation: Incorrect — Span relationships use trace context, not copied stack text.

stem: What is a consequence of head-based trace sampling?

options.label: Every slow trace is guaranteed to be retained
options.explanation: Incorrect — Latency is unknown when the head decision is made.

options.label: No trace context needs propagation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sampling state is commonly propagated with trace context.

options.label: Span timestamps become exact CPU timings
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sampling policy does not change clock meaning.

options.label: The keep/drop decision is made before the complete trace outcome is known
options.explanation: Correct — An early decision cannot condition on a later error or final latency.

stem: Why should high-cardinality secrets or full user tokens not be attached as span attributes?

options.label: They create cost/privacy risk and may expose credentials through telemetry
options.explanation: Correct — Telemetry is widely replicated and indexed, making sensitive high-cardinality fields dangerous.

options.label: Attributes cannot contain strings
options.explanation: Incorrect — String attributes are supported; governance is the issue.

options.label: Trace IDs become mathematically invalid
options.explanation: Incorrect — Attribute values do not alter trace-ID validity.

options.label: Spans with attributes cannot have parents
options.explanation: Incorrect — Parentage and attributes are independent.

stem: Two services have skewed wall clocks, making a child span appear to start before its parent. What should the investigator avoid concluding immediately?

options.label: That the services ran on different hosts
options.explanation: Incorrect — Clock skew is especially plausible across hosts.

options.label: That causality is impossible or instrumentation order is necessarily wrong
options.explanation: Correct — Unsynchronized clocks can distort cross-host timestamp ordering even when context propagation is correct.

options.label: That each span has a duration
options.explanation: Incorrect — Duration can still be measured locally with a monotonic clock.

options.label: That a trace identifier was propagated
options.explanation: Incorrect — The shared trace context may remain valid despite timestamp skew.

sources.title: Hypothesis documentation — What is property-based testing?

stem: What distinguishes property-based testing from a short list of example-based tests?

options.label: It removes assertions from the test
options.explanation: Incorrect — Properties are assertions expressed over generated inputs.

options.label: It proves the implementation correct for every possible input
options.explanation: Incorrect — Finite randomized exploration finds counterexamples but is not generally a formal proof.

options.label: It generates many inputs and checks an invariant that should hold for all of them
options.explanation: Correct — The test describes general behavior while the framework explores concrete cases.

options.label: It measures only throughput under load
options.explanation: Incorrect — Performance testing is a separate purpose.

sources.title: Hypothesis documentation — What is property-based testing?

stem: After finding a failing generated input, what is shrinking intended to do?

options.label: Increase the input until the program times out
options.explanation: Incorrect — Shrinking moves toward simpler values, not larger stress cases.

options.label: Delete the failing test from the suite
options.explanation: Incorrect — The counterexample should be retained or reproducibly regenerated.

options.label: Reduce the executable binary size
options.explanation: Incorrect — Test-case minimization is unrelated to compiled artifact size.

options.label: Find a simpler failing example that preserves the bug
options.explanation: Correct — A minimal counterexample is easier to understand and reproduce.

sources.title: Hypothesis documentation — What is property-based testing?

stem: Which property is suitable for a serializer and parser intended to be inverses?

options.label: parse(serialize(x)) equals x for every supported value x
options.explanation: Correct — The round trip directly checks preservation of the represented value.

options.label: serialize(x) is always the same length
options.explanation: Incorrect — Different values can legitimately require different encoded lengths.

options.label: parse(x) always returns null
options.explanation: Incorrect — That contradicts successful recovery of supported values.

options.label: serialize runs in exactly one instruction
options.explanation: Incorrect — Instruction count is not the functional inverse property.

sources.title: Hypothesis documentation — What is property-based testing?

stem: Why must a property-test generator respect the input domain unless invalid inputs are the behavior under test?

options.label: Generators cannot create strings
options.explanation: Incorrect — Property frameworks commonly generate strings and structured data.

options.label: Out-of-domain cases can overwhelm the test with irrelevant rejections
options.explanation: Correct — Useful generation targets values for which the stated invariant is expected to hold.

options.label: Valid inputs make shrinking impossible
options.explanation: Incorrect — Shrinking can preserve domain constraints.

options.label: Domain constraints turn tests into static analysis
options.explanation: Incorrect — The test still executes generated runtime cases.

sources.title: Hypothesis documentation — What is property-based testing?

stem: A randomized property test fails in CI. What information is especially useful for reproduction?

options.label: Only the total number of passing tests
options.explanation: Incorrect — A pass count does not reconstruct the failing input.

options.label: The repository star count
options.explanation: Incorrect — Popularity has no diagnostic relationship to the generated case.

options.label: The minimized counterexample and generation seed or replay data
options.explanation: Correct — Either the concrete failing case or deterministic replay lets developers rerun the failure.

options.label: The machine’s screen resolution
options.explanation: Incorrect — Display geometry is irrelevant unless it is explicitly part of the input domain.

stem: What feedback does a coverage-guided fuzzer use to retain promising inputs?

options.label: Whether the source file has more comments
options.explanation: Incorrect — Static comment count gives no runtime path feedback.

options.label: Whether every byte is printable ASCII
options.explanation: Incorrect — Binary inputs may be valuable and printability is not coverage.

options.label: Whether execution uses exactly one thread
options.explanation: Incorrect — Thread count is not the core novelty signal.

options.label: Whether an input reaches new code paths or coverage features
options.explanation: Correct — Inputs that expand observed behavior become seeds for further mutation.

stem: What should a good in-process fuzz target generally do for each input?

options.label: Exercise the parser or API deterministically and fail on a real invariant violation
options.explanation: Correct — Fast deterministic harnesses let the fuzzer attribute crashes and explore many cases.

options.label: Write every input permanently to production storage
options.explanation: Incorrect — Persistent side effects slow fuzzing and create unsafe state.

options.label: Catch and suppress all memory errors
options.explanation: Incorrect — Suppressing faults hides exactly the defects fuzzing should expose.

options.label: Require a human to classify every execution
options.explanation: Incorrect — The oracle must be automated for high-throughput exploration.

stem: What is the role of a seed corpus in coverage-guided fuzzing?

options.label: It lists expected CPU benchmark scores
options.explanation: Incorrect — A fuzz corpus contains inputs, not performance targets.

options.label: It provides useful starting inputs that mutations can evolve
options.explanation: Correct — Representative seeds help the fuzzer reach deeper parser states sooner.

options.label: It replaces the crash oracle
options.explanation: Incorrect — The harness still needs to detect failures.

options.label: It guarantees complete path coverage
options.explanation: Incorrect — Seeds improve exploration but cannot guarantee exhaustive coverage.

stem: Why are fuzzing crashes often deduplicated by stack or coverage signature?

options.label: Duplicate crashes repair themselves
options.explanation: Incorrect — Deduplication organizes reports; it does not fix code.

options.label: Only the first crash is reproducible
options.explanation: Incorrect — Multiple crashing inputs can all be replayed.

options.label: Many different inputs may trigger the same underlying defect
options.explanation: Correct — Grouping equivalent failures keeps triage focused on distinct root causes.

options.label: A fuzzer may report only one source line total
options.explanation: Incorrect — Fuzzers can discover many independent issues.

stem: A fuzz input consistently takes far longer than the configured limit without crashing. Why is it still interesting?

options.label: Timeouts prove the output is correct
options.explanation: Incorrect — Runtime duration says nothing about result correctness.

options.label: Slow inputs cannot be minimized
options.explanation: Incorrect — Fuzzers can minimize inputs that preserve a timeout behavior.

options.label: The fuzzer has necessarily lost network access
options.explanation: Incorrect — An in-process target can hang entirely in local computation.

options.label: It may expose algorithmic-complexity denial of service or nontermination
options.explanation: Correct — Pathological inputs can be security and reliability defects even without memory corruption.

stem: Which defect is AddressSanitizer specifically designed to detect?

options.label: A heap use-after-free
options.explanation: Correct — ASan instruments memory accesses and poisons freed regions to catch later use.

options.label: A logically wrong tax calculation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Memory-safety instrumentation cannot infer business rules.

options.label: A missing database index
options.explanation: Incorrect — Query-plan quality is outside ASan’s scope.

options.label: A malformed TLS certificate chain
options.explanation: Incorrect — Certificate validation is unrelated to address checking.

stem: Why is an AddressSanitizer build usually not used as the production performance baseline?

options.label: ASan removes all compiler optimizations by definition
options.explanation: Incorrect — It can be combined with optimization; instrumentation overhead remains.

options.label: Instrumentation and shadow memory materially change runtime and memory cost
options.explanation: Correct — The diagnostic build intentionally trades overhead for memory-error detection.

options.label: ASan executes no application code
options.explanation: Incorrect — The instrumented application runs normally until a violation is detected.

options.label: ASan changes every algorithm to O(n²)
options.explanation: Incorrect — It adds overhead but does not universally change asymptotic complexity.

stem: Which ASan option area helps detect access to a stack variable after its function has returned?

options.label: Leak-only suppression
options.explanation: Incorrect — Leak suppression controls reporting of retained heap allocations.

options.label: Coverage-guided mutation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Mutation is a fuzzer behavior, not stack-lifetime instrumentation.

options.label: Stack use-after-return detection
options.explanation: Correct — The mode preserves or poisons returned stack frames so stale accesses can be reported.

options.label: Link-time symbol stripping
options.explanation: Incorrect — Removing symbols makes diagnostics less readable and does not detect stale stack use.

stem: Why does ASan typically terminate after the first detected memory error?

options.label: Only one memory error can exist in a process
options.explanation: Incorrect — Programs can contain multiple independent defects.

options.label: The compiler forgets all later source locations
options.explanation: Incorrect — Debug metadata remains available; termination is a diagnostic policy.

options.label: ASan licenses permit a single report
options.explanation: Incorrect — The behavior is technical, not licensing-related.

options.label: Continuing after memory corruption can produce misleading cascades and unsafe execution
options.explanation: Correct — The first report is usually closest to the actionable violation.

stem: An ASan report appears only under a particular integration test. What should be preserved for triage?

options.label: The exact input, instrumented binary settings, and symbolized first-error stack
options.explanation: Correct — Reproduction context plus a readable allocation/free/access history makes the lifetime bug actionable.

options.label: Only the final process exit code
options.explanation: Incorrect — The exit code lacks the faulty address and stack history.

options.label: A profile from an unrelated release build
options.explanation: Incorrect — A different workload and binary may not reproduce the violation.

options.label: The average response time of passing tests
options.explanation: Incorrect — Aggregate latency does not identify the invalid memory access.

stem: What is the defining advantage of static analysis over runtime instrumentation?

options.label: It observes real production timing exactly
options.explanation: Incorrect — Without execution it cannot directly measure wall-clock behavior.

options.label: It can inspect program paths without executing a concrete test input
options.explanation: Correct — Static analysis reasons over code and models, including paths tests may not take.

options.label: It eliminates all false positives
options.explanation: Incorrect — Approximating possible behaviors can produce infeasible-path reports.

options.label: It proves every external dependency correct
options.explanation: Incorrect — Dependencies and environment assumptions remain outside many analyses.

stem: What does a path-sensitive analyzer track?

options.label: Only the filename extension
options.explanation: Incorrect — Path sensitivity concerns execution paths, not filesystem paths.

options.label: The chronological order of production requests
options.explanation: Incorrect — That requires runtime telemetry.

options.label: Constraints and state along distinct control-flow paths
options.explanation: Correct — Separating branch conditions helps identify defects possible only after particular decisions.

options.label: CPU sample frequency per function
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is profiling rather than symbolic path reasoning.

stem: A warning describes a path that program invariants make impossible, but the analyzer cannot infer those invariants. How is it classified?

options.label: A false negative
options.explanation: Incorrect — A false negative is a real defect the tool fails to report.

options.label: A benchmark regression
options.explanation: Incorrect — No performance comparison is involved.

options.label: A deterministic crash
options.explanation: Incorrect — The described path is specifically unreachable under the invariant.

options.label: A false positive
options.explanation: Correct — The tool reports a defect that cannot occur in the real program state space.

stem: What does taint analysis commonly track?

options.label: Whether untrusted data reaches a sensitive sink without required validation
options.explanation: Correct — Sources, propagation rules, sanitizers, and sinks model injection-style flows.

options.label: Whether each function has unit tests
options.explanation: Incorrect — Test coverage is not a taint-flow property.

options.label: Whether the heap is fragmented
options.explanation: Incorrect — Allocation layout is unrelated to untrusted-data provenance.

options.label: Whether algorithms are asymptotically tight
options.explanation: Incorrect — Complexity proofs do not establish input sanitization.

stem: Why can a static analyzer miss a defect inside a framework callback or native library?

options.label: Static analysis can read only comments
options.explanation: Incorrect — Analyzers inspect executable program structure.

options.label: Its model may not capture the external code’s control flow or side effects
options.explanation: Correct — Analysis precision depends on available summaries and whole-program visibility.

options.label: Callbacks never execute in production
options.explanation: Incorrect — Frameworks routinely invoke callbacks at runtime.

options.label: Native libraries cannot contain defects
options.explanation: Incorrect — Native code can contain many classes of defects.

stem: In a leak report, what does “definitely lost” memory mean?

options.label: The block is still reachable from a live pointer
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is categorized separately because the program could still access it.

options.label: The allocation was correctly freed twice
options.explanation: Incorrect — A double free is an invalid-free error, not a lost block.

options.label: No pointer to the allocated block can be found at program exit
options.explanation: Correct — Without a reachable pointer, the program cannot free or use that allocation.

options.label: The bytes were swapped to disk
options.explanation: Incorrect — Virtual-memory residency does not determine reachability.

stem: A long-running service’s “still reachable” heap grows without bound across identical requests. Why is that worth investigating?

options.label: Reachable memory consumes no RAM
options.explanation: Incorrect — Reachable objects still occupy virtual and often resident memory.

options.label: Only definitely-lost blocks affect memory usage
options.explanation: Incorrect — All retained allocations contribute to process size.

options.label: Growth proves the allocator is corrupt
options.explanation: Incorrect — Intentional but unbounded retention is another plausible cause.

options.label: Reachable caches or registries can still cause operational memory exhaustion
options.explanation: Correct — Reachability prevents classification as lost, but unbounded retention remains a production problem.

stem: Memcheck reports an invalid read immediately after an object is freed. What defect does that evidence support?

options.label: Use-after-free
options.explanation: Correct — The access targets storage whose lifetime ended at the free.

options.label: A stable sorting violation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Equal-key ordering is unrelated to object lifetime.

options.label: A missing trace parent
options.explanation: Incorrect — Distributed trace topology does not explain invalid local memory access.

options.label: An amortized resize
options.explanation: Incorrect — Dynamic-array growth can be valid and does not imply reading freed storage.

stem: Why is tracking the origin of an uninitialized value useful?

options.label: It makes all reads atomic
options.explanation: Incorrect — Origin metadata does not change synchronization.

options.label: It points toward where undefined data entered the computation, not merely where it was observed
options.explanation: Correct — The first visible bad branch may be far downstream from the missing initialization.

options.label: It converts the value to zero
options.explanation: Incorrect — The tool diagnoses; it does not repair program state.

options.label: It guarantees zero runtime overhead
options.explanation: Incorrect — Origin tracking adds additional instrumentation cost.

stem: When is a narrowly scoped Memcheck suppression appropriate?

options.label: For every warning in the process
options.explanation: Incorrect — Broad suppression destroys the signal needed to find real defects.

options.label: Whenever a test is slow
options.explanation: Incorrect — Performance alone does not make a memory report invalid.

options.label: For a understood, unavoidable report in trusted library code while preserving other diagnostics
options.explanation: Correct — A precise suppression reduces known noise without hiding unrelated application errors.

options.label: Before reproducing the reported stack
options.explanation: Incorrect — The report should be understood before deciding it is safe to suppress.

stem: ThreadSanitizer reports two conflicting accesses to the same location from different threads with no happens-before relation. What has it detected?

options.label: A deadlock
options.explanation: Incorrect — Deadlock is lack of progress due to waiting; it need not involve conflicting accesses.

options.label: A cache miss
options.explanation: Incorrect — Hardware cache behavior does not establish a language-level race.

options.label: A stable ordering guarantee
options.explanation: Incorrect — The missing happens-before relation means ordering is not guaranteed.

options.label: A data race
options.explanation: Correct — Conflicting unsynchronized accesses, with at least one write, satisfy the memory-model definition.

stem: Why will replacing a shared plain counter with an appropriate atomic operation silence a genuine counter race?

options.label: Atomic access participates in the memory model without conflicting non-atomic accesses
options.explanation: Correct — The counter update becomes a defined synchronized atomic operation.

options.label: Atomics make every surrounding data structure immutable
options.explanation: Incorrect — Only the atomic object and specified ordering semantics are affected.

options.label: Atomics force all threads onto one CPU
options.explanation: Incorrect — They coordinate memory operations without requiring single-core execution.

options.label: The increment is removed from the program
options.explanation: Incorrect — The update still occurs; its concurrency semantics change.

stem: A reported data race appears harmless because both threads usually write the same value. Why should it still be fixed?

options.label: ThreadSanitizer reports only deadlocks
options.explanation: Incorrect — Its primary purpose is dynamic data-race detection.

options.label: The unsynchronized conflicting accesses are undefined or invalid regardless of observed equal values
options.explanation: Correct — Coincidentally equal outcomes do not create a happens-before relation or defined execution.

options.label: Equal values make writes read-only
options.explanation: Incorrect — A write remains a write even when the bits match.

options.label: The report proves the compiler is broken
options.explanation: Incorrect — The program violates synchronization requirements; optimizer behavior can expose it.

stem: Why can failing to instrument a linked library reduce ThreadSanitizer’s effectiveness?

options.label: Uninstrumented code cannot run
options.explanation: Incorrect — It can run, but TSan sees less of its behavior.

options.label: The library automatically becomes thread-safe
options.explanation: Incorrect — Omitting instrumentation changes observability, not correctness.

options.label: Synchronization and conflicting accesses inside that library may be invisible to the detector
options.explanation: Correct — Dynamic race detection needs instrumentation around relevant memory operations.

options.label: TSan switches to formal verification
options.explanation: Incorrect — It remains a runtime detector.

stem: A TSan test run is clean. What is the strongest justified conclusion?

options.label: The program is proven race-free for all schedules
options.explanation: Incorrect — One or many runtime executions are not an exhaustive proof.

options.label: The program contains no concurrency
options.explanation: Incorrect — Concurrent code may execute without triggering a detectable race.

options.label: All locks are free of deadlock
options.explanation: Incorrect — Race detection and deadlock proof are different analyses.

options.label: No race was observed in the schedules and code paths exercised by that run
options.explanation: Correct — Dynamic analysis cannot cover executions that the workload and scheduler did not produce.

stem: A microbenchmark’s result is never consumed and the compiler removes the measured computation. What happens to the result?

options.label: The benchmark reports unrealistically low time for work that no longer executes
options.explanation: Correct — Optimizers may legally eliminate computations with no observable effect.

options.label: The benchmark becomes a valid upper bound
options.explanation: Incorrect — Removed work makes the measurement a lower artifact, not an upper bound.

options.label: The algorithm’s output becomes more accurate
options.explanation: Incorrect — Elimination avoids producing the output entirely.

options.label: The timer automatically restores the operation
options.explanation: Incorrect — Benchmark timing cannot force semantically dead code to remain.

stem: Why should expensive input construction often happen outside a benchmark’s timed loop?

options.label: Setup code cannot allocate memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — It can allocate; the concern is measurement scope.

options.label: Otherwise setup cost is attributed to the operation being measured
options.explanation: Correct — Separating fixtures isolates the latency of the target operation.

options.label: Timed loops may execute only once
options.explanation: Incorrect — Benchmark harnesses typically adjust iteration counts.

options.label: Inputs built outside the loop are always cached
options.explanation: Incorrect — Placement does not guarantee cache residency.

stem: A JIT-compiled runtime shows much slower first iterations than later ones. What must a steady-state benchmark account for?

options.label: The algorithm changes its Big-O after compilation
options.explanation: Incorrect — JIT changes constants and code quality, not usually the mathematical input-growth class.

options.label: Later iterations are automatically incorrect
options.explanation: Incorrect — Optimization preserves semantics when the runtime is correct.

options.label: Warm-up, compilation, and optimization phases before measuring steady state
options.explanation: Correct — Early iterations include runtime work absent after code becomes hot.

options.label: Only cold-start latency can ever be measured
options.explanation: Incorrect — Cold and steady-state performance are distinct valid targets.

stem: Two benchmark versions differ by 1%, while run-to-run noise is 5%. What should be concluded?

options.label: The 1% version is certainly faster
options.explanation: Incorrect — A point estimate smaller than noise is not decisive.

options.label: Both versions have identical machine code
options.explanation: Incorrect — Noisy timing does not establish code identity.

options.label: The slower sample has worse asymptotic complexity
options.explanation: Incorrect — Small timing variation cannot reveal a different growth class.

options.label: The evidence does not yet distinguish the versions reliably
options.explanation: Correct — The observed delta lies inside normal variation and needs more controlled samples or statistics.

stem: Why should benchmark input distributions resemble production data?

options.label: Branch behavior, cache locality, and algorithmic paths can depend on input shape
options.explanation: Correct — Synthetic easy cases may exercise a materially different cost profile.

options.label: Production data makes timers perfectly accurate
options.explanation: Incorrect — Timer and environmental noise still exist.

options.label: Representative inputs eliminate privacy obligations
options.explanation: Incorrect — Realistic data must still be sanitized and governed.

options.label: Input shape affects correctness but never speed
options.explanation: Incorrect — Many algorithms and hardware effects are data-dependent.

stem: How does git bisect reduce the number of commits tested when locating a regression?

options.label: It benchmarks every commit from oldest to newest
options.explanation: Incorrect — That is a linear scan, not bisection.

options.label: It repeatedly tests a midpoint and discards the known-good or known-bad half
options.explanation: Correct — Binary search over ordered history needs only logarithmically many classifications.

options.label: It merges all suspect commits into one
options.explanation: Incorrect — Combining changes would obscure which commit introduced the behavior.

options.label: It searches commit messages for the word “slow”
options.explanation: Incorrect — Text labels are not evidence that a commit reproduces the regression.

stem: What property must an automated git bisect test command have?

options.label: It must modify every tested commit
options.explanation: Incorrect — The command should observe behavior without rewriting history.

options.label: It must always exit successfully
options.explanation: Incorrect — A constant outcome cannot distinguish good from bad revisions.

options.label: It must classify the checked-out revision reproducibly as good or bad via its exit status
options.explanation: Correct — Reliable automated classification lets bisection choose the correct half.

options.label: It must depend on current network latency
options.explanation: Incorrect — External noise makes classifications unstable and can misdirect the search.

stem: Why can ordinary bisection mislead when a bug is introduced, fixed, and reintroduced within the candidate range?

options.label: Git hashes stop being unique
options.explanation: Incorrect — Commit identity remains unique regardless of behavior transitions.

options.label: The midpoint cannot be checked out
options.explanation: Incorrect — The logical assumption, not repository access, is the issue.

options.label: Benchmarks cannot return exit codes
options.explanation: Incorrect — A wrapper can classify measurements using an exit status.

options.label: The good/bad property is not monotonic along history
options.explanation: Correct — Binary elimination assumes a single transition between known endpoints.

stem: When should a commit be marked “skip” during git bisect?

options.label: When it cannot be tested or its result cannot be classified reliably
options.explanation: Correct — Skipping avoids treating build failures or inconclusive measurements as evidence.

options.label: Whenever it contains many changed files
options.explanation: Incorrect — Change size does not make a revision untestable.

options.label: Whenever the revision is bad
options.explanation: Incorrect — A reproducibly bad commit should be marked bad, not skipped.

options.label: Only for the initial known-good endpoint
options.explanation: Incorrect — Any untestable candidate may need skipping.

stem: A performance bisect points to different commits on repeated runs. What should be stabilized first?

options.label: The alphabetical order of commit authors
options.explanation: Incorrect — Author names cannot affect execution measurements.

options.label: The benchmark environment, workload, and good/bad threshold
options.explanation: Correct — Noisy classification violates the reliable predicate bisection depends on.

options.label: The number of branches in the repository
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unrelated refs do not change a checked-out commit’s benchmark.

options.label: The color of terminal output
options.explanation: Incorrect — Presentation has no bearing on classification stability.

stem: In a heap snapshot, what does a retaining path explain?

options.label: Which CPU instruction allocated every byte
options.explanation: Incorrect — Allocation stack and retaining path answer different questions.

options.label: The exact wall-clock time until collection
options.explanation: Incorrect — Reachability does not predict when a future collection will run.

options.label: Why an object remains reachable from a garbage-collection root
options.explanation: Correct — The reference chain identifies ownership preventing collection.

options.label: The object’s network round-trip time
options.explanation: Incorrect — Heap references do not encode request latency.

stem: Why are detached DOM nodes retained by JavaScript references a leak signal?

options.label: Detached nodes execute faster than attached nodes
options.explanation: Incorrect — Rendering attachment is not a performance guarantee.

options.label: The browser deletes all event listeners immediately
options.explanation: Incorrect — References and listeners can be part of what retains the node.

options.label: DOM nodes are stored only on disk
options.explanation: Incorrect — They consume process memory while alive.

options.label: They are no longer displayed but cannot be collected while references remain
options.explanation: Correct — Application state keeps otherwise obsolete UI subtrees alive.

stem: What tradeoff does allocation sampling make compared with recording every allocation?

options.label: Lower overhead in exchange for statistical rather than exhaustive allocation data
options.explanation: Correct — Sampling keeps profiling practical while estimating hot allocation sites.

options.label: It proves there are no unsampled leaks
options.explanation: Incorrect — Unobserved allocations prevent exhaustive guarantees.

options.label: It records object contents without privacy risk
options.explanation: Incorrect — Sampling frequency does not sanitize captured values.

options.label: It removes garbage collection from the runtime
options.explanation: Incorrect — The application continues to allocate and collect normally.

stem: A memory timeline repeatedly rises and drops to the same baseline after GC. What does that pattern suggest?

options.label: There can be no allocation performance cost
options.explanation: Incorrect — Short-lived objects can still create CPU and GC pressure.

options.label: Temporary allocations are being reclaimed rather than accumulating across cycles
options.explanation: Correct — A stable post-GC floor is unlike an obvious unbounded retention trend.

options.label: Every object lives forever
options.explanation: Incorrect — The drops demonstrate substantial reclamation.

options.label: The process uses constant resident memory
options.explanation: Incorrect — Heap usage can vary and OS residency can follow different patterns.

stem: Why compare heap snapshots after repeating the same workflow and forcing comparable GC points?

options.label: It guarantees identical object addresses
options.explanation: Incorrect — Compaction and new allocations can change addresses.

options.label: It turns the heap into a CPU flame graph
options.explanation: Incorrect — Heap snapshots describe objects and references, not sampled stacks.

options.label: Growth in surviving object groups can reveal unintended retention per iteration
options.explanation: Correct — Controlled before/after snapshots separate retained state from transient allocations.

options.label: It removes the need to inspect retainers
options.explanation: Incorrect — Growth identifies suspects; retaining paths still explain ownership.

stem: A request is slow but its thread has almost no samples in an on-CPU profile. What is the next useful hypothesis?

options.label: The request necessarily performs no work
options.explanation: Incorrect — Waiting can dominate latency even when CPU work is brief.

options.label: The profiler proves the network is healthy
options.explanation: Incorrect — Absence of CPU samples does not identify the waited-on resource.

options.label: The algorithm must be O(1)
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU sample count does not establish input-growth complexity.

options.label: The thread spends time blocked, sleeping, or waiting off CPU
options.explanation: Correct — CPU profiles omit much of the latency when execution is not scheduled.

stem: What does an off-CPU stack trace recorded at descheduling help identify?

options.label: The code path that initiated the blocking wait
options.explanation: Correct — The stack at sleep or block time points to locks, I/O, timers, or other wait sites.

options.label: The exact instructions executed while asleep
options.explanation: Incorrect — A descheduled thread executes no instructions during the wait.

options.label: Only the thread that wakes it
options.explanation: Incorrect — Wakeup attribution is separate from the blocked thread’s own stack.

options.label: The compile-time type of every heap object
options.explanation: Incorrect — Stack samples do not enumerate object types.

stem: Many off-CPU samples accumulate below a mutex acquisition. What is the strongest immediate inference?

options.label: Removing the mutex is automatically safe
options.explanation: Incorrect — Correctness invariants must be preserved before changing synchronization.

options.label: Lock wait contributes materially to observed latency
options.explanation: Correct — The aggregated blocked duration is evidence of contention at that acquisition path.

options.label: The lock holder is always the same thread
options.explanation: Incorrect — Blocked stacks alone may not identify holder identity.

options.label: All CPU cores are fully utilized
options.explanation: Incorrect — Threads can wait on a lock even with idle cores.

stem: A handler uses 5 ms of CPU but completes in 500 ms. Why is optimizing instructions alone unlikely to remove most latency?

options.label: CPU time always equals wall time
options.explanation: Incorrect — Blocking and scheduling make them diverge.

options.label: The handler has no dependencies
options.explanation: Incorrect — Long waits often indicate dependencies or contention.

options.label: About 495 ms is spent waiting or unscheduled rather than executing instructions
options.explanation: Correct — The gap between CPU and wall time dominates the end-to-end duration.

options.label: Instruction optimization increases network distance
options.explanation: Incorrect — CPU tuning does not change physical network path length.

stem: What does measuring time from a thread becoming runnable until it actually runs reveal?

options.label: DNS resolution time
options.explanation: Incorrect — DNS may make a task blocked, not runnable on a CPU queue.

options.label: Heap reachability depth
options.explanation: Incorrect — Object-reference chains are unrelated to scheduling.

options.label: Static analyzer path count
options.explanation: Incorrect — Run-queue delay is observed at runtime.

options.label: Scheduler run-queue latency
options.explanation: Correct — The task is eligible but waits for CPU service during that interval.
